title: Records of Wang Fengyi’s Excellent Words
excerpt: 15. The Way of the Maiden, the Daughter-in-law, and the Old Woman

inline.s: The venerable good man Wang Fengyi (

) was a hired farmhand in the countryside. He never went to school, yet because he earnestly practiced loyalty and filial piety, he came to understanding through sincerity. At thirty-five he set out to rescue his friend Yang Bai, and midway, in the black night, he saw the bright day and understood the Way. At thirty-eight his father passed away; he kept vigil at the grave for a hundred days and attained great awakening. He then devised the method of healing illness through the principle of the nature, explaining illness to transform the world and universally delivering the multitude.

When the good man Wang spoke of the Way, his words seemed homely and plain, yet their meaning was profound, all flowing forth from his own nature; unbound by scriptures and teachings, he taught with expedient means, lively and natural. His words are fit not only to serve as a standard of conduct, but as a great and world-spanning law. His essential aim was to teach people to fulfill the way of loyalty and filial piety, to transform their nature, and to establish their destiny. He practiced “setting aside the habitual nature, transforming the inborn nature, and completing the heavenly nature,” and “stopping the karmic destiny, finishing the yin destiny, and increasing the heavenly destiny.” The good man Wang often said, “Whatever nature a person has, that is the destiny he has. The wood nature draws misfortune, the fire nature suffers, the earth nature bears toil, the metal nature meets poverty, and the water nature is wronged. (These are the five yin natures.)” He also said, “Those of the realm of body are marked by lowliness, those of the realm of mind by poverty, those of the realm of intention by wealth, and those of the realm of will by nobility.” This shows that a person’s wealth and honor or poverty and lowliness, good fortune or misfortune, suffering or joy all lie in his own hands. Whoever would see the whole leopard, let him read this book.

What is good? What is evil? To act in accord with principle is good, and to act against principle is evil; to do a thing well is good, and to do it badly is evil; to harbor a public heart is good, and to harbor a selfish heart is evil.

There are three great kinds of wicked people in the world, and thieves and robbers are not counted among them. Those who preach the Way but do not practice it, who know their faults but do not mend them, are wicked people of the first rank. Those who feel wretched at suffering a small loss and delighted at gaining a small advantage are wicked people of the second rank. Those who know that what is not their due cannot be had, yet brood on it without cease, and who know that unlawful things must not be done, yet do them in secret, are wicked people of the third rank. Beyond these, those who are pleased when praised and displeased when criticized are all people who are not good.

To be happy at gaining an advantage and angry at suffering a loss — such a one is not a good person. Someone who learned the Way from me was reckoned a good man too, but he had stored up much grain: when drought came and the price of grain rose, he was delighted; when rain came and the price fell, he fretted. Where in that is even a trace of a good heart?
To want to be a good person is very easy: when you see what others do and your conscience cannot bear it, simply do not do the same yourself.
Set yourself right, and the world is right; for once I am good, wherever I go is made good.

A single person is a world, and when I am good, one world is made good. When the Buddha was perfected, a Western Land of Ultimate Bliss was perfected; when Jesus was perfected, a kingdom of heaven was perfected. People today all wait for the world to be good before they will be good themselves, not knowing that when the world truly is good, it will be too late for you to want to be good!

When people read the books of the ancients, they ought to learn from the ancients — that is the right way. People today only read and never learn, and so they have read the books into “loss”! The sages would like to take the books back and stop people from reading them! If you resolve to learn from the ancients (from the sages and worthies), then in time the people of the world will have to read you. Set an example for later generations, and when the world of Great Harmony comes, everyone will learn from you — that is reading you. In reading books and learning the Way, what matters is practice: keep yourself low and your resolve great; join yourself to the ancients (join to their spirit), and you too are an ancient.

People know only that one should read much and read until it is familiar, not that one should put the books into practice. That is like studying a map until you know the bearings of every place, yet never going there — how then can you see the real scenery? Or like memorizing a cookbook without ever eating the dishes — how then can you taste the true flavor?

People today have read a great many books and know of many ancients, and yet they think highly of not one of them and find not one to their liking, so they learn from not one of them. That is to look up to oneself; yet one is forever throwing tantrums and never content, which is again to look down on oneself. To my mind, that is sheer folly!

I never went to school as a child and cannot read a word. But whenever I heard that some ancient was good, I learned from that one. If I saw a living person who was good, I would not leave his side, watching how he conducted himself. To know one more person is to know one more way. I first learned from “Yang Jiao’ai giving up his life to fully preserve friendship” and went to rescue Yang Bai; next I learned from “Yang Yi keeping vigil at the grave” and kept vigil at my father’s grave for three years. For each thing I undertook I learned from one ancient, and that ancient’s spirit came to aid me. This was my “to learn and constantly practice it,” and it accords exactly with the sages’ Way. It is a pity that the world does not believe it truly and will not go and learn; meeting a good person, they pay no heed — that is learning in vain, with no practice.

Reading books is not as good as reading people; reading people is not as good as reading myself; reading myself is not as good as reading heaven. In ancient times each person had one book to read; they could recite it but not use it, and the book was a book while the person was a person — that is “the one root scattered into ten thousand particulars.” Now we do not use books but speak only of the Way, and this is called “reading myself.” Once one has read himself clear, he goes and practices it; this is “the ten thousand particulars returning to the one root.” The one is the Way of Heaven — this is reading heaven.

Reading books is not as good as reading people: take one person as a single character, one family as a sentence, one village as a chapter, one county as a book, one province as a whole volume. A single character has many explanations, and a single person has many affairs — this is what is called reading people.

A scholar who had earned the licentiate degree under the former Qing dynasty said to me, “The ancients said that within books there is gold; yet I have passed as a licentiate and am still poor — the ancients deceived me!” I said, “You have read a great many books, but how many sentences have you put into practice? If you do not act according to the books, it is not the ancients who deceived you, but you who have deceived the ancients!”

Someone asked, “In my early years I studied books but did not dare aspire to sagehood or worthiness; today I learn the Way but dare not learn to be a Buddha or an immortal. I have heard the good man say that one can become a Buddha on the spot — I do not know whether I can or not.” I told him, “Those who study books are intimidated by the sages and dare not go and learn; those who learn the Way are intimidated by the Buddha and dare not take a step. The sages, worthies, immortals, and Buddhas of old were all made by human beings. You too are a human being; if you can learn from him, you are him — what is there to doubt?”

What makes a sage a sage is simply that he urges people to learn the Way. If we wish to learn to be sages, we need only urge others — what is so hard about that? The sages of old perfected the Way by teaching, and teachers today also teach — why have they not perfected it? The sages taught people to learn the Way regardless of whether they had money, making the teaching of people their first concern. Teachers today know only how to earn money and do not care whether a person is perfected or not. I say the difference between a sage and an ordinary person lies exactly in this.

When we know a person, we know only the general look of his face, and that is enough to know who he is — how could we make out every limb and hair of his? Understanding the Way is like this, and reading books is like this too. If one can read the first chapter of the Great Learning until it is clear, all the ways of being human are known. If one can read the first chapter of the Doctrine of the Mean until it is clear, the Way of Heaven is wholly understood, and becoming a god or a Buddha, a sage or a worthy, takes no more than that. It is a pity that people spread themselves wide and let their fields go to waste!

In his old age Confucius spoke with his disciples about their aspirations, and he wished that “the old might be comforted and the young cherished” — but he only spoke of it and did not accomplish it. I have founded many homes for the aged and gardens for the young, and so have repaid Confucius’s great vow on his behalf. When Confucius transmitted the Way, he taught only men and did not teach women; my founding of schools for women fills up Confucius’s gap.

To harbor the Buddha’s heart, speak the Buddha’s words, and do the Buddha’s deeds — to become true in one’s very being — that is to be a Buddha. Most people who would learn the Buddha’s way today apply their strength at “wishing to make bright virtue shine throughout the world,” not knowing that one must begin with “cultivating the self, rectifying the mind, making the intent sincere, extending knowledge, and investigating things” — and so they cannot become Buddhas.

People do not understand the meaning by looking at the name, and do not know that “my Buddha” is myself. They insist on seeking outward, and the more they seek the farther off it is. So the ancients said: “Seek not the Buddha far on Vulture Peak; / the Vulture Peak is in your mind to seek. / Each person has a Vulture Peak tower; / there cultivate, hour by hour.”

People today are all pinned down under a great big hat: those who learn Buddhism suppose the Buddha to be one of a kind, one whom no one else can learn to be. If someone says he wants to learn to be a Buddha, they take him for a madman and think it an insult to the Buddha. In truth such people make the Buddha small! If everyone practiced the Buddha’s way and everyone were a Buddha, how wonderful that would be! The Buddha wishes that all people may become Buddhas — he is not content merely to have become a Buddha himself.

In the Buddha’s heart there is not only the wish that everyone may become a Buddha, but the wish that they may be several grades higher than the Buddha. A person, too, must teach others to stand higher than himself before he can be said to have done right by them.

Ordinary people think that others’ affairs have nothing to do with them, and so they pay no heed. They do not know that others are myself and I am others — self and other are originally one body. Only one who has realized the oneness of self and other is a person of the Buddha realm.

It is said that in the Buddha land, when one person has food to eat, everyone has food to eat, and when one person has something to use, everyone has something to use. Why is that? Because there is no distinction between self and other. So only one without the distinction of self and other is a citizen of the Buddha land.

To learn goodness is to learn “good,” and to learn the Way is to learn “the Way” — you cannot afford to confuse the two. So-and-so opens his mouth and it is all about the Buddha, while I speak only of myself. The Buddha is a person’s model; only by doing as the Buddha said can one become a Buddha. To talk of the Buddha every day and speak of the Buddha all day long, showing off how much one knows — that is learning goodness (having much knowledge), not learning the Way; it is like a blossom that will set no fruit.

People all recite the name of the Buddha who is already accomplished; I recite the name of the Buddha not yet accomplished, that he may become a Buddha — that is true Buddha-recitation. Who are the Buddhas not yet accomplished? Everyone in the world. When I urge a person to fulfill the way of being human, that is reciting him into Buddhahood. Do they not know that a Buddha is not made by reciting in vain? He is one who has slipped out from amid contention and greed. I neither contend nor am greedy, and I urge others neither to contend nor to be greedy — and the crowd still does not believe it. How laughable!

The Buddha was made by a human being, yet today people do not seek the way of being human; they seek the Buddha’s way first — truly grasping the far and letting go the near. I obtained the Way from carrying out hired labor (working as a servant), and people all looked down on me. One year a certain gentleman spoke a Chan riddle to me: “A mustard seed can hold Mount Sumeru.” I said, “That is me.” He said, “Please explain.” I said, “This person living in the world is indeed as tiny as a mustard seed, and yet within my heart are stored four great worlds: the Buddha land, heaven, the sea of suffering, and hell. Is that not speaking of me?”

The eight virtues (loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, love, trustworthiness, righteousness, harmony, and peace) are eight gates, and through any one of them one can enter the Buddha land. But a person should enter by the gate that is his to enter — this is the meaning of “acting within one’s own position.” I entered by two gates, loyalty and filial piety: in herding cattle and working as a hired hand for others, I held firm to the single word “loyalty”; toward my elders I held firm to the single word “filial piety.” This I dare to be confident of.

People do not attain the Way because nature, mind, and body have not become one. When the body works while the mind thinks of other things, mind and body are not one. When one cannot bear adversity and gets angry and hot, nature and mind are not one. Only when the three are one can one attain the Way. To become a Buddha, the four realms must also be made one (see “29. The Four Realms” for details). People today recite the Buddha’s name with the mind only, while body and speech run counter to the Buddha — how can they become Buddhas?

In my early years of urging the world to goodness, I did not dare carry books, for fear people would ask me what religion I belonged to. Whatever religion I met, that was the religion I was. That year I went to the Christian church in Chaoyang, and someone asked me what religion I was. I said, “No religion.” He gave me a good mocking (sarcasm and ridicule): “No religion? And were you not taught by your father and mother?” In truth the principle is one, but if a person is not genuine, it is hard to perfect the Way.

Before doing anything, a person should first listen to the tone of heaven. What the crowd approves accords with the heart of heaven; what the crowd opposes goes against the will of heaven. Who says heaven cannot speak?

In your dealings, never wrong others, for to wrong others is to wrong heaven; never deceive others, for to deceive others is to deceive heaven; never doubt others, for to doubt others is to doubt heaven. If you do not believe in heaven, heaven will not bless you.

Would you see the heart of heaven? First look at the hearts of the crowd. Would you hear the words of heaven? First listen to the words of the crowd. Would you know the will of heaven? First examine the will of the crowd — the crowd is heaven.

The crowd is heaven; therefore speak according to the principle of heaven and act in accord with the hearts of people. To nurse a grievance is to resent heaven; to follow selfish interest is to defy heaven; to cultivate the nature is to serve heaven — this is called the oneness of heaven and humanity.

The petty person in his doings loves to cheat heaven, because he acts behind people’s backs and dreads their knowing; but in the end he cannot hide from people, which is to say he cannot hide from heaven. If he cannot deceive the heart, neither can he deceive the earth.

Suppose there is a rebellious, unfilial son who beats his own father and mother, and not anyone else’s; yet everyone hates him — this is heaven hating him. Again, suppose there is a filial son who is devoted to his own father and mother, and not to anyone else’s; yet everyone respects him — this is heaven respecting him.
The one who curses and beats others is surely disliked by the crowd; the one who is cursed and beaten is surely pitied by the crowd. This is precisely where the heart of heaven shows itself.

Human beings and heaven are connected through and through: to accord with the human way is to accord with the heavenly Way. Follow heaven, and heaven responds; defy heaven, and calamity falls. To think the heavenly Way unreliable is not to know heaven.

To take the heavenly destiny as sovereign is to settle accounts with heaven. If a person believes in heaven, heaven will never fail him. To be unable to trust people is to be unable to trust heaven. If you do not trust others, others will not trust you.

My Way is the Way of the crowd, and to believe in the crowd is to believe in heaven. Only when a person can handle affairs before heaven, speak before heaven, settle accounts with heaven, and act according to the principle of heaven does he accord with the Way of Heaven.
If you mean to be good, the crowd will take you in hand — and it is not the crowd that manages you, but heaven. Let those who learn the Way take note: when heaven takes you in hand, do not get angry!

Only one who has gained the Way of Heaven can enjoy the blessings of heaven. The Way of Heaven is far off, and to know heaven is very hard; but drawing back, to know the nature is the shortest road. Within the nature there is heaven, and destiny is the human world. Know people and know the nature, and you know heaven — why seek far away? Why must people study heaven? Because when they do not accord with the Way of Heaven and have left heaven behind, they are either willful or given to blaming others, and so they invite calamity and contract illness.

The Way gave birth to heaven and earth, heaven and earth gave birth to human beings, and human beings received the spirit of heaven and earth and are their representatives. Heaven cannot speak, but a person can speak; earth cannot act, but a person can create. I say that heaven and earth are myself, and that is the Way as well. All things are mine, and yet they are not mine. A person is as great as heaven and earth; only one who can take the heart of heaven and earth as his own heart is one body with them and can commune with them. As it is said, “The good he will surely know beforehand, and the evil he will surely know beforehand.” Only because people are obscured by the desires of things do they think they are not in touch with heaven and earth; and so when calamity comes they do not know it, and when virtue comes it gives them a fright.

The nature is the Way of heaven, and sincerity is the heart of heaven. To fulfill the nature is to serve heaven: fulfill one part of the nature and you know one part of heaven; make sincere one part of the intent, and you know one part of the heart, you grow one part in the principle of heaven, and you remove one part of human desire. Fulfill the nature to the utmost, and you are one body with heaven!

One who gains the Way of Heaven may be said to have joined himself to heaven; knowing when to advance and when to withdraw, with nothing hanging on him and nothing in his way, he can be “self-possessed in whatever situation he enters,” one body with heaven and earth.

A person is originally one body with heaven and earth. If there is anything you do not understand, only seek it of heaven, and there is nothing you will not obtain. If there is anything that goes against your wishes, or a wrong you have swallowed without redress, only speak it out to heaven, and it will of itself be settled.

Whatever a person is deluded by, by that he suffers harm. So the rich die by their wealth, the noble die by their rank, and the amorous die by their passion. Only one who can break free has the Way; one who cannot break free is a deluded person.

People say that the hu, huang, bai, and liu spirits (the fox spirit, the weasel spirit, the hedgehog spirit, and the snake spirit) can delude a person. I say the world is one vast deluding maze, and there is not a single thing in it that does not delude. The upper sort are deluded by principles, deluded by letters or by religion; the middling sort are deluded by fame and profit, by sons and daughters; the lower sort are deluded by wine and lust, and to the end of their lives cannot break out of the maze; the lowest sort are deluded by ghosts and gods, by food and clothing, and when they die that is the end of it — truly pitiable! Only by distinguishing clearly among the four realms (see “29. The Four Realms” for details) can one be free of delusion.

Everyone in the world is deluded by ghosts! Those who nurse grievances are plagued by the ghost of wrongful death; those who get angry, by a fierce ghost; those who get hot, by a hasty ghost; those who blame others, by a ghost of enmity; those who cannot keep their nature steady, by the ghost of impermanence. Beyond these, the lover of wine is deluded by the wine ghost, the lover of tobacco by the tobacco ghost, and the lover of lust by the lust ghost. Whoever has an inborn nature and a craving is being toyed with by ghosts! There is no ghost that toys with a spirit.

People of the world who learn the Way are deluded by the Way as well. Hearing that someone has spiritual powers, they go and revere him, bowing their heads to the ground before him; hearing that some immortal is efficacious, they set up an offering and burn incense to him; hearing that some deity is good, they build him a temple, thinking it boundless merit. How is this different from the flattery of a petty man? That is called delusion. And those who act from a greedy heart, seeking blessings, are even farther from the Way! So I say: he builds temples, I cultivate the spirit; he builds houses, I build people.

Some are deluded by wealth and lust, some by tobacco and wine, some by sons and daughters: having none, they long for them; they adopt a son from a relative, they take in a daughter, and then they contend and covet on their children’s behalf, forgetting the way of filial piety — and so the world goes bad. Those around me are deluded by me, they revere me and exalt me, saying I have the Way. In truth I have deluded no one; people insist on being deluded by (believing in) me.

Everyone says that chanting scriptures is cultivating goodness — but if one only chants and does not cultivate, how can one be good? A vegetarian is called a good person, yet in truth vegetarianism merely cuts off the cycle of retribution: if you do not eat them, they will not eat you. Burning paper money is said to settle grievances, but if a person’s own grievances cannot be settled, how can the grievances of ghosts be settled? That year I was in Jinzhou, and Old Uncle Qiu chanted a mantra for a whole morning. I asked him what he was chanting. He said it was a mantra for resolving grievances, able to settle them. I said that if one can refrain from blaming others, one can settle boundless grievances.

Whoever throws a tantrum has something to lean on: the noble throw tantrums leaning on their rank, the rich leaning on their money, the poor leaning on their poverty, little children leaning on their youth, and those who have founded a livelihood leaning on the fund that supports them. All are deluded people. It would seem that making a great fortune and holding high office are no good thing either: burdened by fame and profit, deluded by fame and profit, one is better off without them and lighter for it. Only one who can be amid fame and profit yet stand outside them counts as having come out of the common run; he is a true person.

Some people in the world superstitiously consult the eight gates: whenever they are about to leave the house or take up a task, they must examine the eight gates. Others superstitiously consult the eight characters, often inviting a blind fortune-teller to cast their horoscope. To my mind, “filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame” are the finest eight gates, and if a person walks through these gates, there is no eight-character fate that could be bad; they suffice for becoming a sage or a worthy. Still, one must also see which gate is the one for him to enter and go in by that gate. I entered by the gate of loyalty: from childhood I herded cattle for others, as I grew up I worked as a hired hand for others, later I farmed at home, joined the lecture hall to urge people to goodness, and founded free schools for women and the Moral Society. I dare say there was not one of these that I did not carry out with loyalty and sincerity. Once the one word “loyalty” is there, the other seven virtues are not lacking — how then could my eight gates and eight characters be bad? Why should people be superstitious?

I have often pondered: to blame others is a sea of suffering. The more you blame others, the more wretched your heart grows, until you either fall ill or invite calamity — is this not a sea of suffering? To manage others is a hell: manage them one part and they resent you one part; manage them ten parts and they resent you ten parts — is this not a hell? One must turn it around. Only one who can guide others can settle the debts of human life and fulfill the way of being human. One who can ferry others across is a spirit; one who can perfect others is a Buddha.

The noble person seeks within himself; the petty person seeks from others. When the noble person lacks virtue, he blames himself and cultivates himself; when the petty person has faults, he blames others. He does not blame with his mouth but blames in his heart, and the more he blames the more wretched his heart grows. The grievance that is kept in the heart is poisonous; stored there it not only brings misery but also causes illness — it is in effect swallowing poison oneself. If one can reflect and find one’s own faults, one will naturally cease to blame outward. If you are able, do not blame the unable; if you know, do not blame the ignorant. One who understands the way of facing people will not blame others.

People today are unhappy because others look down on them. But as for me, good is good and bad is bad; what matter whether others think well of me? Just this one thing, not blaming others, is enough to become a Buddha. The clever people of today are forever calculating; and when they tally it up it is either regret or grievance — how can they not fall ill?

The scholar belongs to metal, and metal governs opening up and breaking new ground. In his studies the scholar investigates all things ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign; he is the one who best understands principle, and he is never permitted to blame others. If others do not understand principle, it is because the scholar has not taught them to understand it — how dare he blame them?

The official belongs to fire, and fire governs clear understanding of principle; understanding principle, he does not blame others. If the common people are not good, he blames himself for not having governed and transformed them well — how could he blame others?

The good do not blame others; to blame others is to be wicked. The worthy do not get angry; to get angry is to be foolish. The rich do not take advantage; to take advantage is to be poor. The noble do not throw tantrums; to throw tantrums is to be base.
do not blame others” — three words that are wonderfully perfect!

blocks.text: 7. Do Not Get Angry, Do Not Get Hot

inline.s: I have often pondered: when fire runs backward, one spits blood; when anger runs backward, one vomits food. If one can practice the Way and understand the Way, then anger and fire both subside.

To get hot is the “dragon’s croon”; to get angry is the “tiger’s roar.” Only one who can subdue anger and fire can perfect the Way. When someone provokes you, do not get angry; if you get angry, the anger sinks and turns to cold. When circumstances press you, do not grow anxious; if you grow anxious, the fire rises and turns to heat. Both cold and heat can harm a person. The cultivator is not elated by good fortune nor anxious at ill fortune; then anger and fire do not arise of themselves — this is “subduing the dragon and taming the tiger.” If one can subdue them, they serve me; if one cannot, they become a demon.

Anger and fire are two ghosts of impermanence. If one can subdue them, the fire turns into the “golden boy” and the anger into the “jade maiden,” and I myself become a Buddha. If you are provoked into anger, the anger turns to cold; if you are pressed by circumstances into anxiety, the anxiety is fire. One who cannot be master of himself cannot free himself.

As soon as the inborn nature (the temper) stirs, that is fire; as soon as the selfish heart stirs, that is anger. When the ancients spoke of “subduing the dragon and taming the tiger,” they meant bringing “anger and fire” under control. If one can truly control them, is there any realm of the body that will not be perfected?

When the inborn nature takes charge, the ghost comes to run the household. For to get angry and to get hot surely brings illness, and to fall ill is to be struck down by a ghost! When a right thought arises, the spirit comes; when a wrong thought arises, the ghost arrives. It is a pity that people all refuse to be spirits and are content to be ghosts!

To speak in anger is a “ghost” speaking; to speak when hot is a “demon” speaking. If one can examine oneself at every moment and steadily cultivate, one can “subdue the demons and rid oneself of ghosts.”

Cultivators often speak of being “unstained by a single dust.” I hold that only to be attached to nothing at all is to be “unstained by a single dust.” If, meeting something disagreeable, you stir your nature (throw a tantrum), or meeting something that does not go smoothly, you stir your mind — that is precisely to be “stained by dust”!
Anger belongs to yin, and fire to yang. Who is it that makes you unhappy? These two. And it is the will that can transform them.

Fire arises from the heart; as soon as the heart stirs, fire is born. The moment one grows anxious, fire rises; the moment a thought is set in motion, fire scatters outward. If one can still the heart, the fire sinks of itself. For one who does not keep to his own lot, with its extra cravings, the fire is set in reckless motion. If one can let the heart go and not grow anxious on behalf of others, then the fire does not arise — how light and free that would be!

To stir the nature is fire; to be angry in the heart is anger. When the human heart dies, the mind of the Way is born of itself; when the human heart stirs, the mind of the Way is extinguished of itself, and the thought of contention and greed arises. From contention comes anger, and from greed comes fire; anger and fire attack the heart, and one frets all day long — even with wealth and honor there is no pleasure. So the ancients governed the heart as they treated illness. I say: strangle the heart — how much trouble that saves!
If a person is compared to a head of cabbage: to get angry is to be damaged by wind, to nurse a grievance is to breed maggots, and to stir the nature (to throw a tantrum) is to be pelted by hail.

blocks.text: 8. Find the Good, Acknowledge Your Faults

inline.s: Many are those who cultivate goodness, yet few gain its benefits. Why is that? Simply because in their hearts they store only the faults of others — how can they then obtain good?

Finding others’ good is “gathering the spirit”; noticing others’ faults is “collecting the spoils.” To “gather the spirit” is to gather the sunlight, warming the heart and nourishing it; to “collect the spoils” is to store up dark energy, making the heart gloomy and so harming the body. Everyone has good points — even a wicked person has good points; if you cannot find them on the positive side, look for them on the shadow side. Even bandits have the word “righteousness”; but if a bandit sells out his friends, that “righteousness” topples, and he is sure to be caught in the net. Therefore I say that finding the good is a “pill that warms the heart”: wherever you go you will have good connections, and you will be forever free of sorrow.

To keep others’ good ever in the heart is to store yang, and to keep others’ bad ever in the heart is to store yin — these must be clearly distinguished. The foolish love to rely on themselves and to consider themselves right. They do not seek others’ good, and so they are full of resentment, and much resentment means much suffering. The worthy can humble themselves, fearing only that they themselves are at fault, and they love to take what is good in others; so they gain much, and much gain means much ability.

Finding the good gives rise to an inspiring power and connects one with every affinity; it is the root of breaking through karmic obstruction. Store one part of good and you have one more part of sunlight; to gather the sunlight of the crowd is to gather the ten thousand spirits.

Finding the good is true gold. If you wish to find the good, you must make the will your root; amid what holds not a trace of good, you must find the genuine good. When you have reached the point where you can bear it no longer, yet still can bear it — this is “great righteousness reaching to heaven.”

If one can find the good even in a wicked person, resentment dissolves of itself and cause and effect are settled of itself. My old aunt was always at odds with me and cursed me every day. I thought: even a wicked person must have some good, or she could hardly live in the world. I pondered day and night, and at last I found her good point! I said to her, “The nature is the star of blessing, the mind is the star of emolument, the body is the star of longevity. Your heart is kind, you are warm-hearted in any matter, your body is sound, and you have merit toward others too; only your temper will not give way, and that is why you have not enjoyed your blessing.” She was convinced heart and soul. In seeking others’ good, do not argue over who is right: to argue over right is to be far from the Way!

I had a second aunt whose temper was both cunning and fierce; she loved to drink, and after drinking she was sure to curse people. I thought to myself: she is so cunning, and yet she is never ill; I am so kindhearted, and yet I am ill — what is the reason? She too must have a good point, and I have simply not found it. So I made a resolve: if I do not find her good point, I will starve myself to death. I went without food for three days straight, lying on the heated brick bed (the kang) thinking it over, and on the fourth day I found it! Her good point is that she bears no grudges: even if she is in the middle of cursing someone, if a person says, “You are still cursing him! He is desperately ill — go and treat him at once!” (she could practice acupuncture and cure illness), then even at the dead of night she would go. This truly was her great good point, and that is why she is never ill. When I spoke of it to her, not only did she stop cursing me, she became especially fond of me and said I was a person with a good conscience. From this I learned that finding the good is truly the root of walking the Way.

Acknowledging one's faults gives birth to the water of wisdom. Water can blend the five flavors and harmonize the five colors, now square, now round, as occasion requires. If a person can train his nature until it is like water, he has realized the Way. Hence the ancients said, “The highest good is like water.”

Human beings and heaven and earth are one body. All the affairs of the world are our own proper concern. Since the world is not yet good, how can we be without fault? Fault is everywhere — look down and it is there, look up and it is there, open your eyes and it is there, close them and it is there. To see your wife as lacking is the fault of looking down; to see your elders as wrong is the fault of looking up; to see others as wrong is the fault of opening the eyes; to brood in your heart that others are wrong is the fault of closing the eyes. As I see it, whatever Way you do not understand, whatever task you cannot do, is a fault. Only when a person can find his proper duty does he know his faults. When people have lost heavenly principle, grown blind to the Way, and violated the principle of feeling, they still do not know to acknowledge their faults.

One who truly knows the nature of things will surely be able to acknowledge his faults. Even a blade of grass or a tree — one should know its nature; if one misuses it, one has wronged it. If you truly know the nature of things, you need not seek; they will naturally submit to you.

A person who is enlightened makes the heavenly nature his master and serves with the mind of the Way. Not to know one thing is to be unjust to that one thing; not to know one person is to be unjust to that one person. Only when one can think in this way is he an enlightened person.
If you can take your faults seriously and make them real, then of itself the spirit will be clear, the breath fresh, the heart at peace, and the temper harmonious.
To seek the good in others is the light and clear substance that rises and becomes heaven; to acknowledge one's faults is the heavy and turbid substance that settles below and becomes earth.
Acknowledging faults gives birth to the water of wisdom; seeking the good gives birth to the resonant metal.
Seeking the good opens the road to heaven; acknowledging faults closes the gate of hell.
Acknowledging faults is better than taking the “cooling powder”; seeking the good is better than using the “heart-warming pill.”

The Five Elements I speak of are represented by the five words wood, fire, earth, metal, and water, and are the same as the Five Precepts of the Buddhists, the Five Vitals of the Taoists, and the Five Constant Virtues of the Confucians.

The Five Elements of which I speak are the same as the Five Precepts of the Buddhists. To give rise to anger (wood) is killing; to delight in fine clothes and seek to look pretty (fire) is lust; to shortchange someone by a coin when buying (metal) is theft; to love good food (water) is intoxication; to speak a half-lie (earth) is false speech.

The wood nature draws misfortune, the fire nature suffers, the earth nature bears toil, the metal nature meets poverty, and the water nature is wronged — like a treasure bowl, whatever is within gathers to itself. The Most High said, “Disaster and blessing have no gate; they are drawn by man himself.” Not a word is wrong. So I say that good and ill fortune alike are summoned by one's own nature.

The suffering of man lies in his nature! To refuse to yield is yin wood; to love contending over right and wrong is yin fire; to love resenting others is yin earth; to love disputing is yin metal; to love fretting over others is yin water.

The nature endowed by Heaven is called the heavenly nature, and it is without partiality. The nature inherited from one's parents is called the inborn nature, and it varies from thin to thick. The nature acquired after birth is called the habitual nature, and it holds both good and evil. If the heavenly nature is not pure, one cannot be clear; if the inborn nature is not dissolved, one cannot be spiritual; if evil habits are not removed, one cannot stand firm. Within the inborn nature, he who leans to wood speaks with a tongue that jabs; he who leans to fire speaks with a tongue that scorches; he who leans to earth speaks with a tongue that presses down; he who leans to metal speaks with a tongue that scrapes; he who leans to water speaks with a tongue that drowns. When a person can dissolve his inborn nature, the heavenly nature naturally takes charge.

The natures of ordinary people all lean to one side: the fire-leaning contend, the earth-leaning bully others, the metal-leaning wound others, the water-leaning drown others, and the wood-leaning refuse to yield. If one can dissolve this one-sided nature, he will naturally attain the Way.

When one knows where to stop, there is steadiness” is yang wood; “when steady, then one can be still” is yang fire; “when still, then one can be at rest” is yang earth; “when at rest, then one can reflect” is yang metal; “when reflecting, then one can attain” is yang water. The first chapter of the Great Learning speaks the Way of being human completely through! The first chapter of the Doctrine of the Mean speaks the heavenly Way completely through!

True water is the root of the Buddha. The true (yang) wood nature has resolve, can endure humiliation, and can establish all things. True fire is the root of the spirit; fire governs clear understanding of principle, knows the times and the tasks, can transform all things, and is not bound by them. True earth is the root of the Way; it believes in cause and effect, can contain and transform, and can give birth to all things. When others are bad, that is their own cause and effect — do not resent them, and do not worry on their behalf. True metal is the root of the immortal; it can find the good in others, and seeking the good gives birth to the resonant metal, uniting with all in ties of affinity, having righteousness and decisiveness, cutting through every matter as the blade splits the bamboo, and can create all things. True water is the root of the sage; it can acknowledge faults, and acknowledging faults gives birth to the water of wisdom. A nature yielding and gentle can nourish all things. If a person cannot gain the true Five Elements and, clinging to his inborn nature, acts by it, he will die within the Five Elements!

To reach the heavenly time is yang fire; to believe in cause and effect is yang earth; to seek the good is yang metal; to acknowledge faults is yang water; and to be able to bear wrong is the true yang wood — these are the true Five Elements.

In the heavenly time of today, every person's nature contains fire. The fire nature rules greed and loves to contend over principle, which is why strife and greed never end and warfare never ceases. Not to contend and not to be greedy is true yang fire, and only true yang fire can reach the heavenly time. (To reach the heavenly time is to be without contention and without greed.)

An old man who grows melons can tell their quality without tapping them with his hand or smelling them with his nose — one look with his eye and he knows. It is the same in judging people. There was an old woman who, from the day she married, was scolded by her husband until she was old. She asked me why she was always scolded. I said: “Just look at that gloomy face of yours — you deserve to be scolded. Henceforth, when you spin thread or do needlework, often take a little mirror and look at yourself, and see whether there is a smile. Once the smile appears, you will no longer be scolded.” She did as I told her, and her husband not only stopped scolding her but became exceedingly kind to her.

There was an old woman named Qiao who was ill and asked me to speak on her illness. I told her to seek the Way of being an old woman, and if she found it she would be well. So every day she called out: “Where is the true old woman?” After a few days, her illness of many years was healed all at once.

A certain Mrs. Xiang hired a boy servant, but every day she found fault with him. After a long while Mrs. Xiang fell ill and asked me to speak on her illness. I said: “This boy is a dutiful son. At fourteen or fifteen he can already earn money to support his parents. Not only do you not love him, you are vexed by him. Your own son, over twenty, does not study well nor work well, and spends much of your money each year, yet you still love him — your heart is too partial!” The boy, standing in the outer room, heard me say this, came in and kowtowed to me, then went back out to listen. After pondering for a while, Mrs. Xiang said: “He truly is a dutiful son.” The boy came in again and kowtowed to her. Mrs. Xiang's illness was healed on the spot.

A woman suffering from consumption asked me to speak on her illness. When I reached her home I saw her ordering her children about and none of them obeying, and I knew her husband had failed to uphold the Three Bonds. When I explained the reason her children would not obey, I struck the very root of her illness, and the patient began to speak of her husband's faults. I listened for a long while and then took my leave. Outside, I told her husband: “Go back and say to the patient that Mr. Wang says you are quite right. On no account tell her she is wrong — she will surely go on speaking, and when she has finished, the illness will be better!” A few days later I went to her home again and said, “You have finished speaking of everyone else's faults; do you have faults of your own?” She then began to speak of her own faults, and when she had done, the illness truly healed.

A certain woman of the Lian family, surnamed Zhang, had been married a month when her husband went far away from home. Mrs. Zhang then stayed on in her own family's home for a long time and would not return to her husband's family. Her younger brother fell ill and asked me to speak on the illness. When I had learned the circumstances of her family, I said: “Your brother's illness arises from you, but the root of the illness still lies in your mother. It is a daughter-in-law's proper duty that, even though her husband is away from home, she should still return often to look after her mother-in-law. If you can do this, your brother's illness will heal. I have heard the fortune-tellers say: when yin descends, yang is wounded; when yang descends, yin is wounded; when both yin and yang descend, both men and women are wounded. You are the eldest daughter of the Zhang family and will never return to your husband's home — this is called yin descending; how can the eldest son escape being wounded? Moreover, your mother-in-law leads several girls at home from day to day — can her heart not be grieved? A daughter-in-law should share the hardships of her mother-in-law, and only then is it proper. Return home and serve your mother-in-law, and let your parents come often to visit, to show the affection of relatives — only then is it proper.” At these words the mother and daughter wept bitterly. Seeing that they were moved, I said to the mother: “Do you know the cause of your son's illness?” She replied, “I do not.” I said: “In the past you surely spoke of finding another family for your daughter, did you not?” She said, “I did.” I said: “That was the very day your son fell ill. If you can repent, not only will your son's illness heal, but your son-in-law will also return within a hundred days.” At these words the mother and daughter together went before the Kitchen God, burned incense, and repented. Before a month had passed, her son-in-law indeed returned, and her son's illness also healed. This came about because I am clear about the growth and decline of yin and yang, and about the changes of movement and stillness — that is why I dared to speak, and why it proved true.

My wife's brother's wife was gravely ill, and everyone said the case was dangerous. I knew that her illness came from her being dissatisfied with her mother-in-law and her husband. I went to advise her: “Your mother-in-law and your husband are both your heaven. To be dissatisfied with them is to wound heaven. You should know that your mother-in-law's meddlesomeness stems from her wish for your good — how can you be vexed by it?” At this she nodded. I knew her intent had returned, but I also knew she could not yet be cured. I advised my brother-in-law: “Her intent has returned but her heart has not. Her heart is fixed on Lama Tan (who can heal illness); bring him here and she will recover without taking medicine.” He did as I said and she indeed got well. From this one can see that letting go of the mind's obsession is the very wonder-medicine for curing illness.

I had a younger clansman who had very little money and married a woman, and he was overjoyed. His wife originally had an eye disease, but after she came to his home, because her mind was at ease, the eye disease healed. My own daughter-in-law originally had no eye disease, but later she went blind in both eyes. The difference lies solely in contentment and discontentment.

To brood in your heart that others are wrong is a disease of the heart; to lose your temper often in your nature is a disease of the nature. A heart disease must bring on a nature disease, and a nature disease must bring on a bodily disease. If one can turn it around, the illness will heal.

According to my experience in treating illness, an illness contracted at home can only be cured by going out; an illness contracted away from home can only be cured by returning home. Because the illness lies in the heart, and while the matter of the heart is unsettled the illness cannot heal.

Illness is painful, but if you deliberately rejoice, in time true joy will arise, and the yin breath will fly out like a wisp of smoke and a hundred ailments will vanish. As the saying goes, “When the spirit comes forth, the ghost withdraws.” Joy is the spirit, and yin breath is the ghost; when the spirit comes forth, the ghost naturally runs away!
Those who die of illness all have sins. In the primordial world, people die laughing and joyful, so there is no need to weep.

The Way is not far from man. I speak the Way every day, which is to speak of the human being every day — if I did not speak of the human being, where would the Way be? When one studies the Way without singleness of mind, hearing it many times only makes it seem dull; one does not take being human as a serious matter, does not seek one's own faults, and looks only at the wrongs of others, forgetting oneself. From childhood one is a grandson, then a son; with a son of one's own one becomes a father, and with a grandson one becomes a grandfather — yet in a whole lifetime one has not learned to be even one kind of person, nor walked even one road, and so one comes for nothing and goes for nothing! It is here that man is lost, and it is here that the world turns bad.

I find the people of this world laughable. If they are not managing their wives, they are managing their sons; even brothers, sisters, relatives, and friends — anyone with the slightest connection — they want to manage. But they never think of managing themselves. Take your own eyes: because you could not hold down your fiery temper, they swelled up like a big red peach, and in pain you cry out for your mother — at such a time you cannot even manage yourself, and there is no way to stop your own eyes from hurting. See how foolish the people of this world are!

Among the human relations, people love and respect one another, each fulfilling his own Way — all of it is spontaneous. To put it simply: the Way is fulfilled, not demanded. Parents fulfill their kindness, children fulfill their filial piety, brothers and sisters fulfill their fraternal love — all of it must be spontaneous, and only then is it called fulfilling the Way. If they demand the Way of one another, that is all wrong. To fulfill the Way of one's own accord is good; to demand the Way of one another becomes evil. The reason families today are not harmonious is precisely that there are many who demand the Way and few who fulfill it — just as there are more who come to collect debts than who come to repay them; how can there be no quarreling?

The people of today are prone to drift downward. The elders bustle about day and night while the son idles his time away and can do nothing at all — is he not become a “wandering man”? The girls of the family depend on their parents, contending and coveting insatiably, growing resentment day by day; when they marry they demand both bride-price and dowry, ever dissatisfied, resentful of parents and of husband and of parents-in-law, their breasts full of resentment — are they not become “resentful women”? To transform into the world of Great Unity, let there be no “wandering man” in the land and no “resentful woman” in the household, let not the woman lean on the man nor the man rule the woman, let men and women each stand on their own in true equality — then, overthrowing the old custom of men managing outside and women managing within, it may be called Great Unity.

The people of this world truly have no conscience! From infancy they rely on their mother's milk, a little older on their father's support, and the moment they have some ability they cast aside father and mother to support a wife. In wealthy families the children depend all the more on their parents for a living — if short of food they ask for food, if short of clothing they ask for clothing, thinking it only their due — until they have used up or divided up the family property, and then each goes his own way, like a swarm of small spiders that will not scatter until they have devoured the great spider.

The families of old were mutually dependent — man on woman, woman on man, father on son, son on father — until the dependence grew unbearable and they began to resent one another, even to quarrel and harm one another. If families are not reformed, how can there be happiness?

The Way lies in the one who faces you; what is in oneself is the root. Once the root is established, the Way is naturally produced. For instance, an elder brother should ask only whether he himself is generous, and not whether his younger brother is respectful. A husband should ask only whether he himself is righteous, and not whether his wife is obedient. This is what is meant by “establishing the root”; once the root is established, the Way is naturally born.
The people of today would rather sacrifice their own lives than give up managing others — how foolish they are!

A person with a mind and spirit must have thoughts; but his thoughts should “not go beyond his position.” A father should think on the Way of a father, a son should think on the Way of a son — then how could there fail to be families of kind fathers and filial sons?

I often say: keep those close to you at a little distance, and draw those far from you a little nearer. Because those close to you, being near, are easy to bully; and they are your very destiny, so whether good or bad you must accept your lot and can only transform them through the influence of your virtue. Toward those close to you, you must not speak of their good, nor of their bad, nor even think of them; you may only advise, not manage. And even in advising there is a limit: advise your wife once, your children three times, your brothers four times, your friends five times, but your parents without limit. When the near are brought near it is with the heart; when the far are brought near it is with the intent. The spirit holds all things near and, though near, keeps them at a distance; the Buddha holds all things far and, though far, draws them near. Consider how the people of the world have all become near ones to me!

Know where to stop is the same as knowing the measure. Whatever one does in this world, if one does not know where to stop, it will surely come to grief. Meat is delicious, but eaten to excess it hurts the body; cigarettes and spirits are agreeable, but too much spirits makes one drunk. A capable person, doing too much, is worn out by it; snared by affairs, one cannot free one's hand; stuck to by someone, one cannot let go of the heart; burdened by things, one cannot get free. All of these are deluded people. A person does not live for one or two persons alone. There is a measure even to holding office, a measure to growing rich, a measure to running a household, a measure to serving one's parents — and to establish a livelihood for one's parents is the very end of filial piety in the worldly sense. (This is spoken from the standpoint of worldly dharma; if one can persuade one's parents to recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land, ending birth and death and going on to Buddhahood, that is great filial piety.) I say that those who do not know where to stop are all people who do not know the measure.

The Daodejing says, “To know where to stop is to be free from danger.” Yet ordinary people are unwilling to stop in the pursuit of things, and so they do not attain the Way; they all imagine that stopping would ruin things, not knowing that if one truly stops, there is never a reason to be ruined. Not knowing where to stop is like viewing flowers from a galloping horse — one cannot see them truly. One must stop, and only then can one see clearly.

If your children are not good, it is your heart that is not good; if your wife is not good, it is your destiny that is not good; if your parents and brothers are not good, all of these are your destiny. The people of today, not yet good themselves, first hope that others will be good and fear that others will not; seeing others not good, they grieve and fret, even losing their temper and beating and scolding — truly they do not accept their destiny at all!

I am a farmer, and I often see the sorghum growing in the fields. When some stalks are far too tall and others far too short, one can never reap a good harvest; only when they grow even can the harvest be plentiful. A family is the same. Those with ability stand high; those without stand low. If the high remain high and the low remain low, the family is surely not in order; the high must be able to come down to the low, and only then is the family in order.

In keeping a household, a man should know that toward his elders is the heavenly destiny, toward his brothers is the inherited destiny, and toward his wife is the yin destiny. The people of today attend only to the yin destiny and not to the heavenly destiny, which is why the ways of the world have decayed.

Destiny is a name.’ When the name is right, the destiny is right; when the destiny is right, the nature is naturally transformed. So the most important thing in teaching people is to teach the nature and to teach the destiny. Those who act as parents and teachers should often speak of the good qualities of the elders and ancestors; to teach the young without drawing on the elders' good qualities is to run counter to the Way. In the schools of today only knowledge is taught, and moreover they say the elders are old and decayed; having sown this seed, the greater the knowledge and ability of the young, the more they despise the elders — and so has grown up a custom that knows neither filial piety and fraternal love nor courtesy and yielding. People all fear that their days will turn bad, not knowing that it is when the destiny is ruined that the days turn bad.

To love others can be to harm them; to cling to others is to bully them. Parents ruin their own children, indulging them as they please and doting on them without knowing how, till the children no longer attend to their proper work — adding one ne'er-do-well to the family and one idler to the world. The more karma the son creates, the more the father greedily strives for his sake, in truth pushing the son down into hell; yet he says the son is good for nothing and fears he will suffer in days to come, and so even tainted wealth he will greedily seek. What difference is there between leaving such property to one's descendants and leaving them poison? One brings down calamity on oneself and one's descendants bear the suffering — truly, one reaps what one has sown!

Old people, fearing that their children will suffer, buy up houses and land plentifully and make provision enough for the next generation to live on. Such elders are not showing kindness to their descendants but bullying them. They suppose their descendants cannot make a living and have no strength to earn their bread, and so they prepare greatly. Toward outsiders they are mean and stingy, saving up only for their descendants; and the descendants, having learned nothing, can only eat, drink, and play — until in the end they truly have no food to eat and cannot make a living. Is such an elder not laughable? Are such children not pitiable?

Those in the Buddha-land, meeting, feel affinity; those in heaven, meeting, rejoice; those in the sea of suffering, meeting, are vexed; those in hell, meeting, regard each other with enmity. Whoever comes face to face with you, be it grievance or affinity, is cause and effect, and must be recognized. Know that a grievance is something one has stirred up oneself, and an affinity something one has forged oneself. A father amasses wealth and a son scatters it — this is cause and effect on the face of it; if one amasses wealth again, it is the same as pushing one's son down into hell. Those who are wronged and suffer: every bit they bear, a bit is settled. If they end it by death, that is precisely to lose the matter.

Resentment forges grievances, and vexation is a poison. When ordinary people meet with children who are not good, they give rise to resentment. Do they not know that when children are not good it is your destiny that is not good, calling on you to cultivate your destiny? If you do not cultivate your destiny but instead resent your children, you are throwing away your own life! When children err, parents should be tolerant, should guide, should reprove themselves, and should correct themselves; in time the children will reform of their own accord — this is called righteousness. Otherwise, you resent them and they hate you, and in time it becomes enmity. Moreover, children are the bequeathed virtue of the ancestors; to resent them is to insult the ancestors.

Children who are willing to fulfill filial piety come from virtue; those who ruin the family come from karma. To know whether one's children will succeed or fail, just look at whether one's own conduct is virtue or karma.

The people of the world often scold others for “lacking virtue,” and those who hear it grow angry, not knowing to reflect upon themselves. I hold that when one meets with brothers, wives, or children who are good for nothing and shameless, it is precisely because one's own virtue is insufficient; one should strive to do virtue to make up for it, and in time, if they do not change, they will be transformed. If one does not use virtue to mend the matter, then resentment, beating, and scolding are all of no use.

Once a woman came carrying her child and asked me, “What do you think of this child of mine?” I said: “How amusing! You kneaded the dough yourself, you mixed the filling yourself, and you wrapped the dumpling — and you do not know what flour it is or what filling, yet you come to ask me!” This is the same principle as farming: whatever seed you sow, that is the grain you will reap in time.

My son Guohua asked me, “You lead men and women, preaching the Way all the year round and calling it doing virtue — where after all is the virtue?” I said to him: “In my day I worked as a hired laborer and earned seventy strings of cash a year. Now you earn a hundred dollars a month — you are better than I am, and that is my virtue. If your son comes to be better than you, that will be your virtue.” If he had asked further how his son could ever be better than him, I would have told him: set aside six-tenths of your earnings to do good, use four-tenths to keep house, and your son will surely be better than you.

The heads of old families all know how to play the ghost. Risen early, they either scold people or shout at them, even cursing and beating them; he is angry and others are angry too, and anger is the ghost. I can play the spirit: when I see a person is wrong, I simply smile. Joy is the spirit, and when the spirit arises it does not harm others. At the time I say nothing to him; a few days later, when he is pleased, either he asks me or I ask him, and I set the principle clearly before him, and he reforms. Even a child who is disobedient — I say he is obedient, and though he loves to cry I say he does not cry; in time he naturally changes.

People have a human nature, and things (animals) have their own natures. Only by knowing the nature of people can one deliver them, and only by knowing the nature of things can one use them. Apart from the Way of things, one cannot enjoy the blessings of things; apart from the Way of humanity, one cannot enjoy the blessings of humanity. If one tries to manage others, they surely will not submit. One must know how to lead them — praise their good qualities, hold up their bright points — and then they will gladly follow. Toward animals one should also be gentle and must not beat or scold them. People and things are of one principle, and this is “following one's nature.” Yet people always like to manage others and mistreat animals, in truth pushing them and chasing them down into hell.
If an elder recognizes the good qualities of his children, even when he reproaches them they will be glad. Hence it is said, “Seeking the good opens the road to heaven.”

The Way is the heavenly Way, and everyone possesses it — it has never left human beings, for humans are born of Heaven; whenever you seek it, it responds, whenever you use it, it is there. Heaven has not forgotten humankind. Take the case of an elder: if each day he asks how an elder should conduct himself, after a hundred days he is sure to gain his destiny. Whatever Way one does not understand, if only one asks sincerely, there will come a day of understanding. But when a person acts without following heavenly principle and without filial piety toward the elders, he has forgotten Heaven, and Heaven in turn pays him no heed!

To conduct oneself by the will is true sincerity. If a father-in-law is scolded by his daughter-in-law, he should set his resolve and say, “If you can move me to anger with your scolding, then I am not fit to be a father-in-law!” To be able to abide in this is to be a Buddha, and the Buddha is guarded by spirits. To make the intent one's master is joy itself, and joy is the spirit.

After I understood the Way, my wife slandered me, my son defamed me, and my friends broke with me. Because they were of a different realm from me, I did not resent them. That year when I held a meeting at Fanjiatun, my son Guohua opposed me and rejected me, and on the platform, in stern and violent words, he smashed the teaching rod to bits. The crowd was indignant and wanted to discipline my son for me. I said, no! It was because he feared that I would handle things badly that he had come so far to stop me; if I were not his father, he would never have grown so anxious. I am a man of the will realm — needless to say he struck the blackboard; even if he struck me, I would not be moved, and I would assuredly be fit to be his father. If I lost my temper and cursed him and beat him, I would be without the Way!

Children belong to the world; once they have ability, they should serve the world. If, because of their parents, children are kept tied up at home, then on the children's part it is a small filial piety, but on the parents' part it is no kindness at all!

Everyone possesses the Way; there is no need to seek it outside. First one must overcome oneself, and not try to manage others. To manage others is false; to manage oneself is true. If one is not true oneself, the many will not be convinced. Everyone speaks of honoring heaven and earth and of filial piety to parents. I say, to honor heaven one must first purify one's nature, and while it is impure one cannot be filial to one's father; to honor earth one must first cleanse one's heart, and while it is impure one cannot be filial to one's mother. If heart and nature are not pure, to claim filial piety is to be a scold.

Not to know how to be a person is not filial piety; not to know how to do things is not filial piety; to fail to win the admiration of the many is not filial piety. Only when one is a good person, does good work, and earns the admiration of all is one truly filial.

One who knows how to be a person gathers the ten thousand spirits; one who does not scatters them. To investigate the Way of every person you meet and the principle of every thing you see — this is what is meant by gathering the ten thousand spirits. Only when one understands the Way of the person who faces him does one deserve to be called a human being. Not to understand another's Way is to be unjust to that one; not to understand the principle of a thing is to be unjust to that thing. A son who does not understand the Way of a father is unjust to his father. A husband who does not understand the Way of a wife is unjust to his wife. Only by understanding the Way of the one who faces him can one be a human being.

To seek the Way on one side alone is to overcome oneself. One must acknowledge one's own faults and not seek the faults of others. Whether parents are kind or not, only ask whether you yourself are filial; whether brothers are righteous or not, only ask whether you yourself are fraternal; whether others are good or not, only ask whether you yourself are sincere. Sincerity of will moves the Buddha, sincerity of intent moves the spirits, sincerity of heart moves people, sincerity of body moves the animals. If others are not satisfied with you, it is your want of ability. If others do not approve of you, it is your uselessness. If you look down on others, it is your want of measure.

To fulfill filial piety wholly, one must begin with the three realms of nature, heart, and body. If the nature is not transformed, one cannot be filial in nature; if the heart is not sincere, one cannot be filial in heart; if the body is not cultivated, one cannot be filial in body. To fulfill filial piety truly, one must purify the three realms.

People of the bodily realm know only food and clothing, and think that providing food and clothing for their parents is filial piety — this is filial piety of the body. People of the heart realm understand the feelings of others and take pleasing them as filial piety — this is filial piety of the heart. People of the two realms of heart and body are given to anxious brooding over others and take brooding over their parents as filial piety; but little do they know that to long for one's parents without longing for the Way only increases their sins — if your heart is uneasy, how can the hearts of the elders rest? People of the intent realm make joy their master and take making the elders happy as filial piety. People of the will realm are not bound by forms; they hold the will of their parents in their hearts, and set them at ease so the elders need not worry — this is filial piety of the will, and it is true filial piety. If one can establish a livelihood for the elders and send them to the Buddha-land, only then has filial piety reached its end!

To brood anxiously over your parents with a worried heart is the same as killing them. If you can cut off worldly affection and fulfill filial piety through the will, only then are you a filial son of the Buddha-land.

To have many anxious thoughts is called not knowing good from ill. To brood over the elders in your heart is worse than scolding or beating them. To do what is not your proper work is to wrong heaven, and that is unfilial.

People often ask me how filial piety is to be fulfilled. I say: fulfill it by starting at the places where there is a leak. Wherever there is difficulty, that is where the parents' hearts are troubled; if you do not take charge of it, you cannot be said to have fulfilled filial piety.

If the elders have any faults, it is filial piety only when the children can make up for them. While my mother was alive, fearing that the family would bully us and that her children and grandchildren would be burdened, she dared not support the elderly. Later I knew this was a wrong step, and I at once brought my grandfather back to be supported by me — taking no field for his old age and even shouldering debts — and I must support him; this is precisely the mending of a leak.

The body is a possession, the heart is the children, the mind is the parents, and the will is the grandparents. If you wish to know whether your children are good, look at whether your heart is upright. When a person is unhappy and easily grows dull and sullen, it is because the mind is not sincere, and then the parents are sure to fare ill. So I say, bringing order to the world also begins with oneself.

A certain man asked me, “My father likes to gamble and visit brothels, which harms his body and squanders his wealth. What should I do?” I told him: “You can only use the method of transforming him through influence. I had a clan uncle who was once like this. My younger cousin asked me what he should do. I told him always to speak of his father's good qualities before others — that he can bear loss and has virtue; after a long while the words would reach his father's ears. Then, when his father was in good spirits, he was to prepare some wine and food and serve them to his father, and when his father was pleased, say to him: ‘Everyone says you are given up to idleness. I am your son, and I must resolve to walk the Way and restore your good name.’ He did as I said, and my clan uncle not only returned to the right path but also managed the household with diligence and thrift, adding greatly to his lands.” So I say, to transform the old through influence is the supreme method of filial piety.

To be a poor human being is to be unaware of one's destiny — this is called losing one's destiny. To fail in one's affairs is to be unaware of the Way — this is called losing the Way. Both are unfilial persons. If you wish to deliver your parents from suffering, you must be more capable than the elders yourself and surpass what your parents have done; only then is it true deliverance.

If a person takes the elder's money to buy food, clothing, and supplies to support the elder, it looks like filial piety but in truth cannot be counted as such. If the elder has property, yet the son still worries the elder by earning money, that is also not filial. What I mean is this: if the elder has money, use the elder's money; if the elder has none, let the children earn money to establish the elder's livelihood, so that contention and greed are stopped and virtue preserved — this is true filial piety.

When I was keeping watch at the grave, I knew that the most suffering beings in the world are women, and so I resolved to establish free schools for women, so that women might grow in knowledge and ability; and I founded the Moral Society to teach women to study the Way, so that they might understand principle, support themselves, and not burden men. This was to raise the status of women, and precisely to teach women to escape suffering and attain happiness. The ancients said, “A woman without talent is virtuous.” This saying is utterly unjust! If women do not study, how can they understand principle? It is because they bear muddle-headed children that the world is not at peace. In ancient times there were Three Mothers of the Zhou, and from them were born sage rulers and enlightened kings; and it was only through a mother such as Mencius's that we have Mencius. To reform the seed and keep what is good, and to re-found the root of humanity, one must begin with the education of women. In the future, when the Great Unity comes, women too will hold office and govern the state; whatever men can do, women can do also. Relying not on men, they will naturally not be wronged by men — this is truly to escape suffering and attain happiness.

In ancient times women were not allowed to study, and people said, “A woman without talent is virtuous.” This saying is utterly unjust! If women do not study, how can they understand principle? And if they do not understand principle, how can they walk the Way? That is why I resolved to establish free schools for women, to rescue the women of the world and lead them out of suffering to happiness. First I had my own wife go to study, and afterwards I founded the free schools. At that time the officials would not permit it, and the schools were often broken up; when they dissolved them in one place, I went elsewhere to open them. Later the state also established schools for women, and my aspiration was fulfilled. I also founded the Moral Society, so that women might understand the Way and exhort the world to virtue. This too burst the heavens open; it had never happened before. My son said I was ‘fond of showing off and doing the outlandish,’ not knowing that my teaching of women was precisely a turning over of the world.

The sages of old taught only men, and may be said to have first ‘opened the heaven.’ Now my teaching of women is the later ‘opening the earth.’ From this point on, ‘when adversity reaches its extreme, good fortune comes’; women can all understand the Way, dissolve their inborn nature, nurture their heavenly nature, know sincerity of intention, and keep their minds unmixed. Whatever mind a woman holds, that is the kind of child she bears — without a hair's breadth of error.

When a man transforms his nature, heaven becomes clear; when a woman transforms her nature, earth becomes tranquil. With heaven clear and earth tranquil, the child they bear will surpass a divine prodigy.

In this life, the first thing we must not do is to be superstitious. When everyone honors me and believes in me and says that I have the Way, that too is a superstitious remark. The Way is something every person already possesses; keep to your proper role and act, and you are in accord with the Way. For instance, a woman should study Mencius's mother. She could stand on her own and teach her son, and is a model for women of all ages. If you women resolve to follow her, are you not a second mother of Mencius? And is not the Way of Mencius's mother your own Way?

Women suffer much because they are not contented; they like to compare upward, and when they see others have something they want it too, unaware that their own lot differs from others’. It is thus that custom is ruined. She takes no care whether her husband is in difficulty; she must wear her ornaments! She makes light of persons and makes much of things! She thinks it right that a man should labor for her. Toward her husband she is either watching him or ruling him; at the least she takes the man over, at the worst she wears him to death. Abandoning her parents-in-law, she leads her husband away to live a separate life, and following her own will — how can she be without sin?
