Even if she bears children, it is hard for them to become noble.

The Way lies below, not above; high places are perilous, and only in low places is there the Way. A person who can stoop from honor to lowliness and descend from the high to the low is able to produce nobility; to lift up the foolish is to be a worthy person. Consider Teacher Liu Jingyi. She had originally been a pure cultivator; when she understood the Way of women, she was willing to marry the foolish and clumsy Li Yongcheng. She reached out her hand and took him, without any effort. To bend downward and lower oneself produces nobility; to covet upward is always to be unsatisfied; to shrink small and gather in makes one solid and full; to spread out large makes one thin. When another is stronger than you, you cannot produce nobility — she did not deem Li Yongcheng's stupidity a fault, and that is to be a worthy person.

Worldly people all know how to advance but not how to retreat, like soldiers who enter a battle array and cannot break out of it — how can they avoid harm? It is like a daughter-in-law: before she marries she does not understand the Way of her husband's family, and after she marries she does not recognize the virtue of all its members. This is precisely knowing how to advance but not how to retreat, and so they leave the Way. Having left the Way, they still wish the family to flourish and their descendants to prosper — is this not ‘climbing a tree to seek fish’ [asking the impossible]?

If love were not heavy, one would not be born into this Sahā world; were there no karma, one would not take birth in a woman's body. Since one is born human, one should walk the Way of humanity; when the human Way is fulfilled, the heavenly Way returns. The pity is that people do not understand! They only wish to enjoy blessings and do not know to fulfill the Way. Eating and dressing one's way toward death, profiting the world nothing — this is to abandon oneself. Solitary yin does not generate; seeking vexation on one's own — this is to reject oneself. Human beings are born of yin and yang, and the Way lies between yin and yang. When one understands this, one naturally has no suffering; but to dread suffering yet not fulfill the Way is precisely to oppose heaven — how can one then accomplish the Way?

The most bitter in the world is the widow. In old times, when the husband died, a woman who preserved her chastity was called worthy; but that too does not accord with the Way. There are those who should keep the vow and those who should not. If the parents-in-law are aged and no one serves them, or the children are young and no one raises them, or the nature loves quietness — then she may keep the vow. But if the parents-in-law are still in their prime and there are uncles and elders, and she has no children and is still young, she need not keep it. If she is loath to part with wealth and honor, that is called keeping wealth; if she dreads the suffering of remarrying, that is called keeping the body; and if she is vexed all day long with diseases clinging to her, that is keeping suffering! Only when she walks the Way can it be called keeping chastity.

When a man dies and leaves his parents behind midway, he too has fallen short of filial piety. The one who keeps the vow must be able to fulfill the filial duty on her husband's behalf, and only then does she accord with the Way. So the widow's responsibility is even greater. How can she presume upon herself and wrong others? How can she lose heart and abandon her resolve?

blocks.text: 15. The Way of the Maiden, the Daughter-in-law, and the Old Woman

inline.s: A maiden's nature is like cotton, her will is the root, her mind holds the good qualities of all, her body has the power to help, she takes as her duty the lifting up of the whole family, and she becomes the family's star of honor.

A daughter-in-law's nature is like water, her intent is the root, her body should be diligent, her heart feels gratitude for the whole family's kindness, she takes as her duty the supporting of the whole family, and she becomes the family's star of joy.

The old woman's nature is like ashes, her will is the root, her body should be steady, her mind holds the Way of all, she takes as her duty the encompassing of the whole family, and she becomes the family's star of blessing. This is the true Way of womanhood. Do not despise these words as vulgar; whoever penetrates them will enjoy blessings. Never treat them as a mere mantra that one recites and thinks it done! Only by putting them into practice can one be said to have attained the Way.

To have the will as root is to be without greed; to have a nature like cotton is to be without contention. When cotton is spun into thread it is continuous and long, and the intent of a maiden should also be that enduring.

For a maiden in the family, having the power to help in body dispels the yin destiny and joins her breath with the Buddha-land; holding the good qualities of all in mind joins the ties of affinity and is the path to becoming a spirit; a nature like cotton, with its gentle spirit ever arising, is the root of becoming a spirit; and the will as root is the root of becoming a Buddha.

The maiden is the source of the world! If the source is not muddied, the stream flows naturally clear. If a maiden is given to shrinking back and is unwilling to speak of the Way of the maiden, it is like having a lamp without light.

A daughter-in-law's nature is like water; her temperament should be as gentle as water. Water flows winding and turning, and who knows but that it runs on for several thousand li and finally returns to the great sea — so too should the daughter-in-law's intent be that enduring, lifting up the whole family like water bearing things along. She who knows how to be a daughter-in-law will surely bear noble children. Look at the water! It can nurture all things without contending with them; it dwells in the lowest place, now square now round as occasion demands, blending the five colors and harmonizing the five flavors while its original substance never changes. If a daughter-in-law can make her nature like water, how can she fail to accord with the Way? Following either poverty or wealth, able to be high or low, never changing its own nature — if a person can be so, she has attained the Way and is a daughter-in-law Buddha.

A daughter-in-law should have real practice in her bodily realm, hold the good qualities of the whole family in her heart, and, with a nature like water, be ever joyful. Even when she is wrongfully beaten or wrongly scolded, she must say it is for her good — if they had no thought of her, how could they discipline her? If she meets a husband whose eyes are diseased, let her think that it is far better than having a blind one; thinking so she can be content and always happy. This is the true Way of womanhood. Why is the Way lost? Because ‘each kind of person’ no longer speaks ‘that kind of Way.’

Zhao Boxin of Jinzhou taught in the free schools for women when she was young. Later she married into the Wang family. Her father-in-law was blind in both eyes and of a violent temper; her mother-in-law was a notorious shrew and also smoked opium; and her husband was given to no proper occupation, idle and shiftless, until he drifted away and disappeared. Her mother-in-law abused her in every way, calling her at night to fetch tea and water and serve her till midnight, while by day she still had to teach to support the whole family, never getting enough to eat. Thus she passed more than twenty years, and at last transformed her parents-in-law. Not only did they cease to dislike her, they grew fond of her. When they died she buried them according to the rites, and everyone admired her ability to walk the hard-to-walk Way and endure the hard-to-endure suffering. So I say she was the ‘woman scholar laureate.’

Zhao Boxin practiced the Way most truly. She taught to support her parents-in-law, and in life and in death she fulfilled filial piety completely. She also taught to support her son, and was a loving mother in the human world. If she could further establish herself in the Way, exhort and transform the people of the world, and make no plans for her son, then she would be a mother in the spirit realm. The reason people cannot attain the Way is only that they cannot break through the barrier of children.

Qin Fang Hailan was a woman of heroic spirit. To support her old mother she gave herself as a concubine; to preserve her chastity she disfigured her face to repel the demon; to study the Way she joined the Society while ill; to save the world she taught the Way and discoursed on virtue; to accomplish the Way she bore all toil and blame. People call her an incarnation of a bodhisattva; I say she is a bodhisattva in incarnation. Know this: the Way is cultivated in adversity, and virtue is perfected amidst suffering; break through the hard barrier and you at once reach the other shore.

Du Zhu Yushan is both the very top (the highest) and the very bottom (the lowest, like the sole of a shoe). She is a benefactor and also an old woman. In the family she is the very top — being an old woman, she must know the Way of all the members of the family. As a benefactor she is the very bottom — she must be able to catch the family's failings, knowing the Way of people in the world. Only when she can make clear the Way of each person in the family and the Way of people everywhere can she encompass the family and encompass the world, and discharge her duty of being both the very top and the very bottom. When one family is good, the nation is good; when the nation is good, the world is good. If one can gain the Way of an ancient one, one is an ancient one; gain the Way of a living person and one is a living emanation. To have the will as root is to arrive at the Buddha-land; truly to be able to make the nature like ashes is to be a Buddha.

blocks.text: 16. The Way of Husband and Wife

inline.s: What is the Way? It is yin and yang. What are yin and yang? They are husband and wife. When husband and wife each keep to their proper position, they accord with the Way. Once the Way falls into the acquired world, the man has no true strength and the woman no true gentleness; the family is not harmonious, there are no good descendants, and the harm reaches society — this is why the world is not at peace and the earth not secure. It is all due to the bad root of humanity. I teach husband and wife to understand the Way: when heaven and earth are fixed in their places and the breaths of yin and yang are smooth, the descendants will surely be worthy, and the world will abound in worthy people — how could it fall into disorder again?

The Three Bonds of which the ancients spoke are “the sovereign is the bond of the minister, the father the bond of the son, the husband the bond of the wife.” The Three Bonds of which I speak are: first, the bond of nature; second, the bond of the heart; third, the bond of the body. To lose one's temper is to overturn the bond of nature; to scold is to overturn the bond of the heart; to strike is to overturn the bond of the body. The character for bond should be understood as ‘to lead’; but today people insist on reading it as ‘hard,’ and to display the hard strength of heaven they bully women, turning leading into ruling, making women into slaves and playthings. They do nothing but beat and scold, and still think it is right — truly this goes too far! That is why I advocate the primordial marriage (the marriage of thrift), so that men and women may be equal.

The Three Bonds of which I speak are: not to move one's inborn nature is the bond of nature; not to stir up selfish desires is the bond of the heart; to have no bad habits is the bond of the body. A husband may only lead and teach his wife; he must not rule the woman, for as soon as he rules he is no longer a bond! To scold a woman is to put on a show of authority; though she dares not reply, the anger is already stored in her heart. To beat a woman is to give vent to a murderous spirit; though she dares not strike back, the hatred is already stored in her heart. This anger and hatred, if not vented at the time, will surely be transmitted to the children later on — is this not the great harm of ruling a woman? People are so used to it that they do not notice; truly they are pitifully foolish!

The Three Obediences of which the ancients spoke are: obey the father at home, obey the husband when married, and obey the son when the husband is dead. To obey whether right or wrong is called blind obedience. The women of today have Three Dependencies: at home they depend on their parents, when married they depend on their husband, and in old age they depend on their children — this is also not right. I say a woman has a true Threefold Obedience: the nature obeys heavenly principle, the heart obeys rightful principle, and the body obeys the principle of feeling. That is why I advocate saving money and establishing a livelihood, in order to strike down the Three Dependencies and make a woman a person who stands on her own.

I often say that in discussing morality men and women must each keep to their proper position. A man takes upright firmness as his root. What is firmness? Firmness is not to move one's nature (not to lose one's temper). What is uprightness? Uprightness is to accord with rightful principle. A woman takes gentleness as her root. What is gentleness? Gentleness is to make the nature like water. What is harmony? Harmony is to accord with principle. So upright firmness is gentleness, and gentleness is also upright firmness. The words are different but the spirit is the same; it is only that people are so accustomed that they do not notice!

What after all is meant by ‘reaching the other shore’? I say that a man must understand the Way of women, and a woman must understand the Way of men; only then has each person ‘reached the other shore.’

The husbands and wives of today either have the man ruling the woman or the woman ruling the man, or they rule each other and harass each other — truly becoming a ‘hellish family’! I advocate that men and women stand on their own without ruling one another, precisely to transform hell into heaven.

The people of the world are most foolish; either the man rules the woman or the woman rules the man, thinking that because the other is their own person they must keep them under control. This is called ‘seizing men and dominating women.’ Once one dies, the man marries again and the woman remarries, and neither rules the other. People contend and covet endlessly over property and goods, yet when they die they must abandon it all — if this is not folly, what is? In short, all of it comes from the heavy weight of self-centeredness.

The Way of husband and wife that I teach is the way of yin and yang. When husband and wife are harmonious, the breaths of yin and yang are smooth and they do not overcome each other; not only do they avoid illness and premature death, but the family is well ordered and descendants flourish. So I say that a man must understand the Way of a woman, and a woman must understand the Way of a man, and only then can the family be harmonious and joyful. People today have men ruling the woman and women depending on the man; men beat women and women resent men. This is called the disharmony of yin and yang — how can the family be happy?

Wang Fuqian, explaining the Book of Changes, said: “Heaven One generates water, and Earth Six sustains it.” I asked him: “Water governs gentleness; you are always losing your temper, so how can you count as ‘Heaven One generates water’?” Zhu Xuntian asked me: “How should these two lines be practiced?” I said: “When a man holds to the bond of nature and does not lose his temper, that is ‘Heaven One generates water’; and when a woman can support the whole family, then she may be said to ‘sustain it with Earth Six.’”

A man is a man because of a woman, so a man must understand the Way of women. A woman is a woman because of a man, so a woman must understand the Way of men. If a man has no woman he becomes a widower, and if a woman has no man she becomes a widow; then they can no longer be called a man and a woman!

Before marriage, both men and women make filial piety their chief concern. After marriage, the man makes fulfilling the Way of the husband his chief concern, and the woman makes fulfilling the Way of the wife her chief concern. If a man cannot lead his wife onto the Way — cannot honor his parents above and teach his children below — then however completely he is filial himself, the elders will not be at ease. If a woman after marriage cannot help her husband perfect his virtue, then however filial she is to her parents-in-law, the elders will not be at peace. So whether man or woman, one must understand the Way before one can be truly filial.

In the conduct of husband and wife, it is best to say nothing. To say ‘good’ will spoil them and breed pride; to say ‘not good’ will stir up quarrels. Toward an unrelated person one is unmoved whether they are good or bad; if the husband and wife could regard each other as unrelated persons, they would accord with the Way.

Husband and wife of the will realm are beyond feeling; those of the intent realm have diluted feeling; those of the heart realm are entangled in feeling; those of the body realm cling to feeling. Those who cling stir up trouble; those entangled are fearful; the diluted can last; the transcendent are true. Saying nothing of good, saying nothing of ill, saying nothing of coming, saying nothing of going — this is the husband and wife of the will realm.

Husband and wife of the will realm have no reproaches; they are grateful to each other and never resent anyone. Those of the intent realm are joyous; the husband leads the wife to accomplish the Way, and the wife helps the husband perfect virtue, never losing their temper. Those of the heart realm are the ceremonial couple, who end up ruling each other! Those of the body realm are the beating-and-scolding couple, for since they rose through wealth and power, they turn out badly.

The noble person seeks from himself; the petty person seeks from others. I say that to seek from oneself is the primordial, and to seek from others is the acquired. The husbands and wives of the future should have the husband not seek from the wife and the wife not seek from the husband; each does their own work and fulfills their own Way. When they should be together they are together; when they should separate they separate. Being together, they do not disturb each other but are harmonious and joyful; being separate, they do not long for each other but are entirely natural. This is the primordial husband and wife.

I often say, look at a woman's intent and you know the man's body; look at a man's heart and you know the woman's body. For example, Wang Sanjie dwelt in a cold cave and suffered, yet in her mind's intent she held that her husband would surely become a lord; and later he truly was enfeoffed as a prince. In Li Xuehui's intent she always thought her husband was an opium-injecting ne'er-do-well, and in the end he truly turned out to be worthless. In my heart I held that my wife would surely become a teacher and my son a scholar, and later it all came to be so — this is an example.
A man accomplishes through resolve (zhi); a woman accomplishes through intent (yi).

Heaven gives everyone blessings when they are born; why are there so few who enjoy blessings and so many who suffer? It is because the customs have swept them along and they have lost the way! When officials take bribes it is their wives who push them to it; when a son abandons his parents and contends with his brothers over property, it is for the sake of his wife; when one breaks the law and loses his conscience, it is all for the sake of his wife. Those without a wife do it to enjoy blessings for themselves. From this it can be seen that women have devoured all the loyal ministers and filial sons, and still think they are helping their men, when in truth they are bullying them.

When a woman helps her husband, she should examine what sort of people he associates with and what sort of words he discusses. If a scholar speaks without righteousness and with a narrow nature, or a man in office speaks without shame and loves bribes, and the woman can exhort and transform him, then she is truly helping her husband perfect his virtue!

What distinguishes me in this life is that for the public good I resolved, after establishing the free schools for women, to look no longer after my wife. Other people may do great good deeds, but they can never help caring for their wives, and so they are not my equal. What distinguishes Zhu Xuntian is that he utterly would not manage his wife. He exhorted her six times; not only did she not listen, she insisted on divorce, and yet he did not move his nature — so he rises above the crowd. Worldly people laugh at him for being afraid of his wife, but I call him the ‘champion’ of the Three Bonds.

In worldly marriage, people of the upper class consider wealth and power, seeking to enjoy blessings; the ordinary class considers property, seeking a means of living. A maiden asks her own family for a dowry and her husband's family for a bride-price, and no one asks for the Way. Women of today, being educated, fear that marrying into wealth will weary themselves, and fear that marrying into poverty will bring hardship; no matter how it is, they are ill at ease, and they are not on the Way. If women do not thoroughly understand the Way, the customs of the age are hard to reform and my Way is hard to walk.

I advocate the primordial marriage (the marriage of thrift). When a maiden marries, let her not take even a single garment from her own family, in order to reform the customs. Once a woman has a man she has a selfish heart and treats her husband as a ‘private possession’; she either rules him or frets over him — that is not right either. So I also advocate that women save money and establish a livelihood, in order to strike down the ‘Three Dependencies.’

To establish a heart for heaven and earth, to establish a destiny for the people, to continue the lost lore of past sages, and to open peace for all ten thousand generations.” As I interpret these words, when a man saves money and establishes a livelihood, curbing contention and greed, and knows how to be a man, he has established the heart of heaven. When a woman saves money and establishes a livelihood without burdening the man, and knows how to be a woman, she has established the heart of earth. Whoever occupies a position and knows how to be the person of that position has established the destiny of the people. Achieving these things is precisely continuing the lost lore of past sages and opening peace for all ten thousand generations.

The age of establishing enterprises belongs to the acquired world; the age of establishing livelihoods belongs to the primordial. To take contention and greed as the chief thing is the acquired; to take humility and yielding as the chief thing is the primordial. In advocating the saving of money, the establishment of a livelihood, and the primordial marriage, I am precisely transferring the people to the primordial world! Those who are transferred over are the primordial people. But if one is nominally in a primordial marriage while still harboring a heart of contention and greed, or after establishing a livelihood the heart is still unsatisfied, then one is still a person of the acquired world. In short, whether within the Society or outside it, whoever acts with will and intent is primordial, and whoever acts with heart and body is acquired. Whether one is primordial does not lie in outward form but in actual practice.

Formerly I advocated the marriage of established livelihood, and now I again select adults to re-establish the primordial world. People all make light of what I do and think it is arrogant. Little do they know that the place where I am held in contempt is the very wonder of my practice of the Way! Now it seems trivial and unimportant, but a hundred years from now they will realize that what I advocated are the most important keys to reforming society.

My grandmother was slow of nature yet kindly, but she was lax in managing the household, and my aunt-in-law did not admire her. My aunt's daughter-in-law treated her even more harshly than my aunt treated my grandmother, and went ten years without speaking to her. My aunt's grandson's wife, ever since she married, never served her mother-in-law for a single day; but when her mother-in-law died, she too became good. From this I knew that if the Way is walked wrongly, the error grows farther and farther!

In a former life, whichever Way among the human relations one fell short of, in this life one is lacking in that relation. One who did not fulfill filial piety in a former life will be without a son in this life; if one fell short in all the human relations, then in this life one is a solitary person.

The Wang family of Tuanshanzi village in Chaoyang county were relatives on my mother's side. At first they operated a coal kiln, but later their sons all took to idleness. When I was preaching the books of virtue and reached their village, he asked me: “What sin have I committed, that all the young men of my family should smoke opium, gamble heavily, and take to no proper occupation?” I said to him: “It is precisely because you were harsh toward the poor that the ghosts of the poor all took birth in your house! Before you became the kiln owner, the workers had a meal of noodles every night. You grudged the expense and changed it to two pieces of bean curd for each man. Then you found buying bean curd unprofitable, so you ground it yourself; where others got a hundred pieces from half a dou of beans, you worked up two and a half sheng to make a hundred and twenty pieces — is this not fleecing the poor? At every New Year and festival your houses slaughtered pigs and sold the meat to the workers; the usual price was twenty cents, yours was twenty-five, and you counted a catty as twelve liang, and they had to buy whether they wished or not. So it was with the sale of tobacco and dried goods too. Because you dreaded poverty and were harsh toward the poor, therefore the ghosts of the poor all took birth in your house! You did it yourself, so whom else can you ask?” When he had heard me out, he went away weeping.

When a noble person insults the lowly, in the future they will surely become lowly; when the rich are harsh to the poor, in the future they will surely become poor. This too is the principle of natural circulation, because you have left the Way of wealth and honor!
If you find others distasteful, others will surely find you distasteful; if you find the foolish distasteful, the foolish will surely also find you distasteful and annoying.

Everything has its circulation, not a hair's breadth off. Not to speak of how one must not wrong others in one's heart — even toward animals one must not be cruel. Though animals cannot speak, Heaven will not tolerate it. That year the soldiers at Liujiazi could not catch the bandits, so they seized an innocent man and beat him until he talked nonsense, insisting that the bandits had fled to my house. They took me and beat me badly, but I bore nobody any grudge and lost no temper. Only when I came to keep watch at the grave did I learn that it was because when I drove a cart I had beaten the draft animals too severely! A sin committed in the bodily realm must be repaid in the bodily realm.

What is unfair in this life was not unfair in a former life; what is unjust in this life was not unjust in a past life. Whoever encounters things and feels wronged does not understand the cause and effect of the three lives.
Look at what nature a person has and you will know how his karma stands. Whatever a person receives in this life has all been accumulated in a former life.

By what nature one has in this life, one knows what one did in a former life. If in this life one has the fire nature, in a former life one must have been an official; if the water nature, a merchant; if the wood nature, a laborer; if the earth nature, a farmer; if the metal nature, a scholar.

One who delighted in hunting or in taking life in a former life will have a high fire nature in this life. One who delighted in defying superiors will have a great wood nature. One who delighted in lying will have a strong metal nature. One who delighted in resenting others will have a thick earth nature.

In the nature of an ox there is the fire of foolishness, and in the nature of a dog there is the yin wood; so it takes on that form and suffers that suffering. If it could dissolve its nature, it too could escape the suffering of an animal!

A certain man asked me: “What will I be reborn as in the next life?” I said: “You will be reborn as a second-rate master, without authority or position, because your heart is empty.” He asked how it could be made not empty. I said: “If the nature holds heavenly principle, the heavenly destiny is not empty; if the heart holds the principle of the Way, the inherited destiny is not empty; if the body fulfills the principle of feeling, the yin destiny is not empty. But if one speaks falsehoods, does false deeds, cultivates false virtue, and only loves empty reputation, then even if one becomes a spirit it is a second-rate spirit, and if one is a wife one is a concubine.”

Human beings are the spirit of all things, and so all things long to be reborn as humans; if they cultivate further they may become spirits or Buddhas. The pity is that people are themselves deluded and turn back into things, and so the cycle never ends.

When a person has deluded thoughts or attachments, the cycle is not ended. If one does not know how to be a human or understand the principle of the Way, the heart cannot be ransomed. If one is not satisfied and not content, the intent cannot be ransomed. If things are not emptied and affairs not made clean, the will cannot be ransomed. One must do one thing and finish that thing, walk one Way and finish that Way; being able to plunge in and yet come out again, without being bewitched by the net of the world, only then can one ransom oneself out.

The heart is the root that creates cause and effect. If there is the least selfish thought or a hair's breadth of attachment, there is a shadow in the heart and one cannot ‘settle the dust’ [of worldly entanglements]. If one cannot settle the dust, it is hard to escape the cycle of rebirth. So one must put to death the acquired heart before one can forever cut off the retribution of transmigration.

There is nothing that does not come from cause and effect. When adverse things come, if one can receive them joyfully and pass through them, thinking they are one's due, then naturally they are settled! If one cannot bear them and harbors resentment, then though the matter passes, in the future adverse things will surely come again — precisely because one endured yet did not settle them.

The yin spirit is received from the earth realm and knows only contention and greed, and so it is benighted. The soul-spirit is received from heaven above, knows the human relations and knows courtesy and yielding, and so it is clear and bright.
(These three realms differ from the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness spoken of in the Buddhist scriptures)

A person is born of the three realms: heaven bestows one's nature, earth bestows one's destiny, and one's parents give one the body; therefore the three realms are said to be the origin of a person. Only by keeping the heavenly principle in the nature, keeping the principle of righteousness in the mind, and exhausting the principle of human feelings in the body can one return to the root and come back to the source. People know only of a body-self, not that in heaven there is a nature-self and in the underworld a destiny-self. When the nature is transformed, I receive the heavenly nobility from the nature in heaven; when principle is clear, I receive the human nobility from the destiny in the underworld. So a single person originally has three bodies — alas, no one knows it!

Keeping the heavenly principle in the nature, one should be gentle; keeping the principle of righteousness in the mind, one should be calm and even; exhausting the principle of human feelings in the body, one should be humble and harmonious.

All teachings take the person as the root. A person has three roots: the root of nature, the root of the mind, and the root of the body. When a person forgets the root, he cannot stand firm — “when the root is established, the Way is born”! The body responds to all matters; for what one cannot do, and for work one cannot finish, one must strive to learn. The mind stores all principles — know yourself and know others, know when to advance and when to retreat; see through it and it is no longer difficult. The nature gathers all spiritual beings: one must understand the heavenly principle, reach the heavenly time, and take the heavenly destiny as sovereign; acting according to the heavenly principle counts as having stood firm.

The three realms of nature, mind, and body are not at peace because there are three thieves within them — first, the inborn nature; second, selfish desire; third, bad habits. If you want the three realms to be at peace, use the heavenly principle to seize the thief in the nature, use the principle of righteousness to seize the thief in the mind, and use the principle of human feelings to seize the thief in the body.

To stir the nature and throw a temper is a sickness of the realm of nature; to dwell in the mind on others' faults is a sickness of the realm of mind; to make plans for the body and love to take advantage is a sickness of the realm of body. If one can turn these around, the sickness is cured.

When the realm of nature is clear there is no temper, when the realm of mind is clear there is no selfish desire, when the realm of body is clear there are no bad habits. If the nature is not clear there is no blessing, if the mind is not clear there is no emolument, if the body is not clear there is no longevity; therefore one must clear the three realms.

I have heard people say, “The one breath of primal chaos transforms into the Three Pure Ones.” I think a single person is precisely the “one breath of primal chaos”: if there is no temper in the nature, that is the nature being clear; if there is no selfish desire in the heart, that is the mind being clear; if there are no bad habits on the body, that is the body being clear — when the three realms are clear, only then has one “transformed into the Three Pure Ones”!

I can cure all the sicknesses of the three realms; one must separate the three realms and clear up the three administrations. If the body has no bad habits, the realm of body has no sickness; if the mind has no selfish desire, the realm of mind has no sickness; if the nature has no temper, the realm of nature has no sickness. The sicknesses of the mind and nature can only be cured by the Way — taking medicine is of no effect. Alas, no one knows it!

The nature is the star of blessing, the mind is the star of emolument, the body is the star of longevity. To eat excessively cuts off blessing, to speak and wound others strips emolument, to wear and dress excessively damages longevity. A person must examine himself at every moment and never be neglectful.

The essential Way of life is to be rid of greed, be rid of contention, and be rid of stirring-up. Greedy, one wrongs the heavenly principle and owes a debt to heaven; contentious, one wrongs the principle of righteousness and owes a debt to the human world; stirring up, one wrongs the principle of human feelings and owes a debt to the underworld. If one commits all three words, one owes debts to the three realms — how could there be a good result!
Greed is an offense, contention is a sin, stirring up is karma.

To love to nurse grievances wounds the mind; not to nurse grievances preserves the mind and preserves the life. To love to regret wounds the nature; not to regret preserves the nature and preserves blessing. To love to resent others wounds the body; not to resent preserves the body and preserves longevity. If a person can not nurse grievances, not regret, and not resent others, all three realms are unharmed.

I also have a threefold daily examination. First, is there any temper in my nature? When someone crosses me, what arises in my nature? Second, does my heart know contentment? Is there any selfishness? When I suffer a loss, what is the flavor in my heart? Third, are my actions right or not? What can I truly do? This is my threefold examination.

I also have a threefold program — namely, keep the heavenly principle in the nature, keep the principle of righteousness in the mind, and exhaust the principle of human feelings in the body. I also have an eightfold list: first, do not be greedy; second, do not contend; third, do not nurse grievances; fourth, do not regret; fifth, do not resent others; sixth, do not be anxious; seventh, do not get hot; eighth, do not lose your temper. If one can do this, it costs no money and no effort — not only does one attain the Way, one can even attain Buddhahood.

If one can bear with patience, the nature is settled; if one knows contentment, the mind is settled; if one is diligent, the body is settled — this precisely is the good state; not being settled, one cannot be well.

A person has three natures: first, the heavenly nature; second, the inborn nature; and third, the habitual nature. The nature bestowed by heaven is the heavenly nature, which is purely good and without evil; Mencius's doctrine of the goodness of nature refers precisely to the heavenly nature. The nature born with a person is called the inborn nature, which is purely evil and without good; Xunzi's doctrine of the evil of nature refers precisely to the inborn nature. The nature acquired after birth is called the habitual nature, which can be good or evil — “near vermilion one is reddened, near ink one is blackened.” Gaozi's saying that the nature can “go east or go west” refers precisely to the habitual nature. If the heavenly nature is not clear one cannot be illumined; to clear the heavenly nature, first remove selfish desire. If the inborn nature is not transformed one cannot be upright; to transform the inborn nature, first remove self-opinion. If the habitual nature is not set aside one cannot stand firm; to set aside the habitual nature, first remove bad habits. If a person can act through the heavenly nature, he will naturally “veil his radiance and mingle with the dust.”

People's held minds differ, changing from moment to moment, so a mother may bear nine children, each different — this is called hereditary nature. Just as pepper seeds are inevitably pungent and sour pear seeds inevitably sour. If one has a bad hereditary nature and can transform it away from this body, this is called “transcending upward the nine ancestors”; and no longer transmitting it to descendants is “benefiting downward the seven generations.”

A person's nature is born of himself: whatever he does, that kind of nature is born. Doing good, one gives birth to a good nature; doing evil, one gives birth to an evil nature — it all lies with the person himself.

One who acts through the heavenly nature finds others' good points; one who is ruled by the inborn nature is sure to see others as wrong. Of whatever kind this nature is, it attracts that kind of occurrence.

The heavenly nature has a source and the inborn nature has a root; the habitual nature of the previous life is the inborn nature of this life. If one can transform away the inborn nature (anger, hatred, resentment, vexation, and annoyance), the heavenly nature becomes complete. The one who cannot transform it erupts at the slightest touch, as if possessed by ghosts — hence it is called the “five ghosts,” making the household ill at ease. It is also called the “five poisons,” causing people to fall sick and die. Its root is deepest and not easily pulled out. If a person cannot subdue it, it is hard for him to be a good man. The Buddha said: “Karmic power follows the body and inevitably gives rise to the reckless stirring of ignorance” — it is hard to attain the Way.

The habitual nature is entangled by material desires, and the inborn nature is the affliction of the human world. One who can fulfill his duty in the field of virtue and morality may be said to have escaped the realm of body. One who knows how to be human has escaped the realm of mind. Only when the inborn nature is wholly transformed has one escaped the realm of nature. Otherwise, how could one “transcend beyond the three realms”?
Set aside the habitual nature, transform the inborn nature, and complete the heavenly nature.

A person has three destinies: first, the heavenly destiny; second, the karmic destiny; and third, the yin destiny. The nature accords with the heavenly destiny, and righteousness and duty are the heavenly destiny. The mind accords with the karmic destiny, and knowledge, ability, and wealth are the karmic destiny. The body accords with the yin destiny, and the inborn nature (anger, hatred, resentment, vexation, and annoyance) is the yin destiny. If you study these three destinies clearly and yet use your destiny badly, your destiny is hard to make good. Whether a destiny is good or bad lies with oneself — what need is there to have one's fortune told?

Mencius said, “Cultivate the heavenly nobility and the human nobility will follow it.” But as soon as a person has gained the human nobility, he no longer cultivates the heavenly nobility! Cultivating virtue and the nature increases the heavenly destiny; learning skills and amassing wealth all increase the karmic destiny; contending and greed increase the yin destiny. One who makes good use of the karmic destiny grows in contentment and can dissipate the yin destiny; one who does not know how to use it increases the yin destiny. Only by increasing the heavenly destiny can one surely dissipate the yin destiny. People today know only how to use the yin destiny and to value the karmic destiny, not knowing how to increase the heavenly destiny. How then can they understand the heavenly Way?

Not knowing one's destiny one cannot be a gentleman”; not knowing people one cannot “reach the other shore.” To know people's good points is to know the heavenly destiny; to know people's meritorious deeds is to know the karmic destiny; to know people's inborn nature is to know the yin destiny. Only one who knows destiny is a gentleman. One who readily stirs the inborn nature dissipates the heavenly destiny; one who readily gives rise to resentment dissipates the karmic destiny; one who loves to take advantage increases the yin destiny. When the heavenly destiny is small, you must know how to increase it; when the karmic destiny is small, you must know how to add to it; when the yin destiny is great, you must know how to dissipate it. When the destiny is small you must know how to increase it, and when the destiny is great you must know how to guard it — this is “helding the heavenly authority in one's own hand.”

When someone comes to see me, I first ask what he does and then I know how great his heavenly destiny is. Then I ask about his family property and circumstances, and I know how great his karmic destiny is. I look at the size of his inborn nature and I know how great his yin destiny is. The three destinies are the three realms; with the three realms linked through and through, what is there you do not know?

A teacher must carefully examine the student's heavenly destiny, karmic destiny, and yin destiny, and educate him according to the size of his destiny — only then has he fulfilled the Way of the teacher. Parents can only nurture the body of their children; a teacher can, however, teach the three realms of the student's nature, mind, and body. Comparing them, a teacher is even more important than a parent.

I act through the heavenly destiny, and have dismissed both the karmic destiny and the yin destiny — that is why I am well. People today either use the yin destiny or value the karmic destiny, and fancy their destiny will be good — truly they do not know how to read fortune!

People have no heart for the multitude, but know only of themselves — that is why things go bad. The reason I could become a good man is that I dismissed the heart that was for myself, that is, I strangled the karmic destiny. The karmic destiny is endless and unceasing — is there any limit to pursuing it?
One who acts through the heavenly destiny will surely be good; one who acts through the karmic destiny will surely go bad; one who acts through the yin destiny will surely be destroyed.

My son studied in Shenyang and took third place in the examination, and so I went to the three eastern provinces to teach the Way. His renown from scholarship is the karmic destiny; my teaching of the Way is the heavenly destiny. This precisely is using the heavenly destiny to encompass the karmic destiny — in no case must you let the karmic destiny become greater than the heavenly destiny.
Using the karmic destiny for the public welfare increases the heavenly destiny; using the karmic destiny for one's own enjoyment increases the yin destiny.

One with a great heavenly destiny is not small in karmic destiny either; and one with a great karmic destiny cannot finish the yin destiny. Therefore one should stop the karmic destiny, finish the yin destiny, and increase the heavenly destiny.

One with a great heavenly destiny makes people willingly submit; one with a great karmic destiny receives people's flattery; one with a great yin destiny makes people afraid. One with a great heavenly destiny gets along with others; one with a great karmic destiny oppresses others; one with a great yin destiny frightens others.

Because races differ and customs differ, the teachings founded by the founders of the various religions also differ. Their essential purport is all to carry out the Way on behalf of heaven, and their aim all to ferry across beings, causing people to turn from evil to good, and so to save people's nature and destiny.

Nature and destiny are the root of a person. Once I obtained the human root, the root of the Way is likewise considered obtained. The root of the Way is a person's nature, and the human root is a person's destiny; if the root of the nature is good, then the root of the destiny cannot be bad. From this it is clear that a person's bad destiny is brought about by the burden of his nature. Therefore I teach people to transform the nature; if a person can transform the nature, he may be said to have attained the Way.

The nature is the root of destiny. A person of virtue is sure to have a great capacity of nature; when the capacity of nature is great, the destiny too is sure to be great. A person's destiny is all a good destiny, but because the nature is not good, it drags the destiny down to ruin! What is the Way? It is like the center-line drawn by a carpenter: whether or not others are good, you first draw a center-line for them, take the long and cut off the short, and you accord with the Way.

The Way is destiny, and virtue is the nature. The nature preserves the destiny; destiny has its waning and waxing, and must be preserved intact. If everyone investigates carefully, they will know: all those who make the heavenly nature the master and do not let the habitual and inborn natures run the household have great destinies. Those who do not make the heavenly nature the master, but let the habitual and inborn natures run the household exclusively — their great destinies become small, and their small destinies perish. Truly startling indeed!

The nature is the root and the destiny is the fruit; only when the root is planted can one bear fruit. If a person cannot settle the nature, he has not planted the root; if he does not accept his destiny, it is also hard to bear fruit, like a flower that blooms but bears nothing. One who learns the Way must, first, transform the nature, and second, accept the destiny. When the nature is transformed, one is no longer angry; only when one is not angry will one be willing to suffer loss, and suffering loss is gaining advantage. When one accepts the destiny, one no longer resents others; only when one does not resent others can one endure hardship, and only by enduring hardship can one enjoy happiness. Alas, the world does not know this, and makes light of nature and destiny while making much of fame and profit!

A person's nature and destiny are joined; only when the nature is settled can the destiny stand. In the destiny of being a son, one must settle the nature of a son. In the destiny of being a parent, one must settle the nature of a parent. Whatever the destiny, one must settle the corresponding nature. If one has a good destiny but not a good nature, it is called the nature not returning to the destiny, that is, the nature is not settled. When the nature is not settled, the destiny is ruined. Thus it is: when a person is about to stir his inborn nature, he should first ask himself what his destiny is; then the nature will not dare to move recklessly. This is called “the nature returning to the destiny.” One whose nature returns to the destiny is sure to have his temperament transformed, sure to have his heavenly destiny increase, and sure to be able to become a mature person.

Destiny is like a lamp, and virtue is like the lampshade. Only when a lamp is covered by the shade can it blaze forth great light. A person cultivating destiny must also nourish the nature before it becomes spiritual — the same principle as covering the lamp with a shade.

The Way is like the lamp-wick, and virtue like the lampshade. If virtue is insufficient, one cannot hold off the evil winds of the world; without the Way one cannot blaze forth great light. Therefore it is said: “With the Way but without virtue, one is a demon within the Way; with virtue but without the Way, one is but an empty temple.”

The ancients said: “To cultivate destiny and not cultivate the nature is the first sickness of practice; to cultivate the nature and not cultivate the destiny makes one's single ray of spiritual light useless.” This saying has spoken the importance of cultivating both nature and destiny too penetratingly!

All the world wishes to enjoy happiness. Why are there so few who enjoy happiness and so many who suffer? Because people are, first, not contented, and second, do not accept their destiny. If a person can understand the Way, he will know how to enjoy the blessing he has, and even without blessing he will find it.

Destiny is a person's proper role; keeping one's role, one establishes the heavenly destiny. When the heavenly destiny grows, the name too is sure to grow great. One who knows how to fulfill each role gains that many Ways. If one does not fulfill one's duty, does not exert one's strength, loves vanity, does false things, and has a name without reality, one cannot establish one's destiny. A woman who envies others' good fortune, resents that she is not equal to others, and hates that she is not free like a man, and so nurses grievance or regret — such a one also is not keeping her role.

To see oneself as inferior to others is to deceive oneself, and is also called not knowing contentment; such a person is sure to suffer. A contented person is sure to have his heavenly destiny grow: when the principle of human feelings is sufficient, the principle of righteousness grows; when the principle of righteousness is sufficient, the heavenly principle grows; once sufficient, it requires no effort. If, while doing one thing, one thinks of another, it is called leaking air: like a balloon, once the air leaks it collapses! Or like steamed buns, once the air leaks they are underdone. So the gentleman, in doing things, does not disdain a small matter: with strength for ten, he uses seven, and is both relaxed and cheerful — he is a living immortal. As soon as greed arises one falls into the sea of suffering; however wealthy and noble, one has not the least delight.

A person's name is given by heaven: the one who cooks is called the great cook, the one who writes is called the teacher. If a person's deeds do not match his name, he has lost the heavenly destiny, which is also to be ignorant of his destiny.

In walking the Way one must not leave one's own station; if one leaves one's station, not only is one's labor without result, but one incurs fault besides. What is one's station? It is a person's proper role: “to act within one's own position” one may attain the Way.

A person should act within his own position, not overstepping his station in deeds, not overstepping his station in words, not overstepping his station in thought; only then can he realize the true in his very self. If one, being of the female body, envies men; if a poor person longs for wealth and honor; if while doing one thing one thinks of another — these are all people who have left their station; how can they attain the Way? Just as a pear must ripen on the pear tree and cannot ripen on the apricot tree. If you see that some fruit tree is good, you can graft its scion (the branch to be joined) onto my tree, and naturally it will bear good fruit. Just as a student who emulates the deeds of the ancients is grafting onto the ancients (is joining a branch with them), and thus becomes as one of the ancients.

An eggplant ripens on the eggplant sprout, and a cucumber ripens on the cucumber trellis. Move an eggplant onto a cucumber trellis and it cannot ripen; move a cucumber onto an eggplant sprout and it cannot ripen either. A person, too, must not leave his station; only then can he realize the true in his very self.

For a governor, the people of the province are his destiny; for a county magistrate, the common folk of the county are his destiny; for a teacher, the students are his destiny; for a swineherd, the pigs are his destiny. If, because affairs are many, one gives rise to resentment, or if one relies on power to bully others, that is to throw away one's destiny! If there were no pigs, who would hire a swineherd? If there were no students, who would invite a teacher? If there were no common folk, no officials would be appointed. From this it is clear that the affairs within one's role are a person's heavenly destiny.

There are people whose nature returns to the destiny, and people whose destiny returns to the nature. “Destiny means name.” One who does not act willfully, but according to his name and station discharges his duties with constancy from beginning to end, is called “the nature returning to the destiny.” One who disregards his name and station, acts willfully, begins and stops at random, and is given to sudden joy and anger, is called “the destiny returning to the nature.” Like the parents of great Shun, who wished to harm him: he did not stir his nature and to the end fulfilled filial piety — this precisely is “the nature returning to the destiny.”

Only when the mind holds the principle of righteousness can one know destiny, and one who knows destiny knows his proper role. Only when the nature holds the heavenly principle can one know the nature, and one who knows the nature knows the great Way. There are people whose nature returns to the destiny, and people whose destiny returns to the nature. When the nature comes to return to the destiny, see to which destiny it returns: to return to the heavenly destiny is true, to return to the karmic destiny is false, and to return to the yin destiny is bad. When nature and destiny merge into one, sent forth they are the outer king, and drawn back in they are the inner sage.
Being a mature person does not depend on the height of one's position or the size of one's ability; as long as one keeps one's role and can fulfill one's duty, that is a mature person.

When a person falls into the sea of suffering, if there is no one who can swim to rescue him, it is hard for him to get out by himself. For this reason I resolved to save people's nature and destiny. Saving a person's life is but for a moment and still lies within cause and effect; saving a person's nature is eternal — a single rescue through all the ages, eternally cutting off the cycle. Therefore saving a life is the visible and the momentary; saving the nature is the invisible, imperishable through ten thousand aeons. When a person's nature is saved, it is like coming out of the sea of suffering, like climbing to the other shore, never to fall again.

Only when one can know a person's nature can one recognize the person; only when one can know the nature of things can one make use of things — this is joining the graft with heaven. Whatever a person is like, that is the mind he holds, the words he speaks, and the deeds he does; if you see him as wrong, it is because you do not know his nature, that is, you do not understand his Way — and you are sure to be angered by him. Just as the dung beetle loves to roll balls of dung and the weasel loves to eat chicks, so the greedy and contentious love to take advantage. Each kind of person handles the affairs of its own realm, so it is said all are right.

People are deluded by things and affairs, often taking the false as true — this is called not seeing through. That is why they say others are wrong and get angry and hot with others. In truth it is oneself who has not seen through. If one could see through worldly affairs, one would surely laugh — how could one get angry and fight with others? In the beginning I saw that there was not one good person in the world, and so I got angry; my anger grew into a consumptive sore that lasted twelve years, and it nearly angered me to death. Not until the first month of my thirty-fifth year, when I heard a book of good teachings, did I know that getting angry was wrong; I reproached myself before heaven, and my sore healed overnight, and I left hell at once.

I suffered all kinds of blows, and resolved not to get angry and not to get hot; though people mocked me, I did not stir my nature. Anger and heat are two “ghosts of impermanence”; if one can subdue them, turning the heat into the “golden boy” and the anger into the “jade maiden,” and not be overcome by them, that is a Buddha. That year, at the Du family's distillery in Anda County, I met Zhang Mingzhai and Li Chaoqing, and the two of them mocked me (sneered and ridiculed me) for three days straight; every day I listened from morning to night without making a sound. After supper I went with Meng Hanchen to the outskirts, threw back my head and laughed loud, letting out the yin air, and so I was not overcome by it. “To be angry yet not give way to anger dissolves the demons; to have a grievance yet not requite it is practice.” Not a bit wrong.

What comes against one is virtue, and a person must recognize it. Having suffered a loss, you must not speak of it — it must be that you owed him; when the crowd pities you, then your life grows long. If you are beaten and berated without cause, it is also your own sin; once you have endured it, count it as repaying a debt — and you should even be grateful to him, for if not for his beatings and curses, when would my sins be finished? I say even a petty man has his good point: he is the one who presses others to become good, helping them from the opposite side. For instance, Yue Fei was brought to completion by Qin Hui, and Lord Guan by Cao Cao — how could one not be grateful to them?

The blessing heaven adds comes against you, so people are startled; the blessing people add comes smoothly, so everyone knows it. I say everyone in the world has blessing, only they do not know how to enjoy it; when virtue is brought to them, they are afraid and unwilling to receive it. Do they not know that the Way is accomplished in adversity, and that a person is ruined within his own good fortune? Therefore it is said that good is the beginning of bad, and bad is the beginning of good. Look! Meat has a fragrant savor, but when it goes bad it stinks terribly; cabbage is not fragrant, and when it goes bad it does not stink. A fruit is green and does not spoil; when it ripens, its spoiling is not far off! Human affairs are likewise.

If one wishes to be a good man, one must be able to shoulder grievances; only one who can shoulder the grievances of a thousand or a hundred people has deep blessing. When a person does good and receives an evil retribution, people feel it unjust. Do they not know that to suffer insult and grievance can dissipate boundless sins and offenses? Just seek to keep your conscience uncorrupted, and that is enough.

The diamond is the hardest of things, so one must establish a diamond-like resolve. A foolish person, insulted or rebuked by others, does not take it as added blessing, but instead gets angry — this is the vajra fallen! A clear-sighted person who readily gets angry with the foolish is the vajra burst! Only when it neither falls nor bursts can one establish the diamond-like resolve.

To be tempered through the feelings of human life is true learning”. One must be tempered among relatives and friends; once fully tempered, one no longer fears the bump. Like bricks and tiles, once fired through, they are hard; the unfired are like adobe bricks that, on meeting water, dissolve!

Whatever comes before one is all within one's destiny, so when one meets with untoward things and unlikable people, one must be able to bear it. Confucius was cut off from food in Chen, Jesus was nailed to the cross, and the Buddha had his limbs severed — none of them resented anyone; that is true acceptance of destiny. Only one who truly accepts destiny can attain the Way.

In former days, when Zhang Yaxuan heard me speak of “goodness, merit, and virtue,” he abandoned his property to set up schools, and though he suffered insults and encountered demonic obstacles, he never retreated from his resolve — that is called settling the will. I often say that what comes against one is virtue, and one should accept it; if the heart is unwilling, then even having accepted it there is no virtue. If one goes on to seek the cycle of retribution, that is even more wrong!

Why does Li Yongcheng surpass the people of the world? Because he has the Buddha-nature. Whoever orders him about, he says “all right.” Whoever upbraids him, he also says “all right.” So I say he is a person of the Buddha realm. The Buddha takes suffering loss and bearing insult as gaining advantage — precisely the opposite of the world.
A person's inborn nature is like a spider's web: at the touch of anything it sticks fast, yet on meeting fire it dissolves. When the inborn nature meets the true fire (joy), it too dissolves.

If one wishes to illumine virtue, one must have the nature full and round. If one wishes the nature to be full and round, one must kill the mind. If one can play the part of a living dead man, the nature will be transformed.

To give up money is not equal to giving up the body; to give up the body is not equal to giving up the mind; to give up the mind is not equal to giving up the nature. If a person can give up the inborn nature, he may be said to have attained the Way. Therefore I teach people to transform the nature — it is a single rescue through all the ages, the nature-spirit never darkened; that is virtue.

When Teacher He was quitting smoking, I spoke the Way to her every day; the smoking was given up well, and she also transformed her nature. Only then did I know that if one can sincerely speak the Way to a person, one can cause that person to transform his nature.

Everyone has an inborn nature, so one must transform it. When I was young I suffered from a consumptive sore; hearing books of good teachings, I came to understand principle, and only then did I know that my nature had gone astray. I turned toward the fire of clear principle, but unexpectedly went into the fire of haste and became very hasty. A man named Qu in my village fell ill, and I spoke the Way and cured him; grateful for my kindness, he sent me some refreshments. I said to him loudly, “Since you have these things, why not give them to your elder brother — would that not be fulfilling your duty as a younger brother! What do you bring them to me for?” The man Qu was very displeased. Only then did I know I had not reached the true fire. From then on, whenever I met people I would first say I am quick of temper and speak frankly, and beg their pardon. In less than a month, the fire of haste was transformed. This is my process of transforming the nature.

The sickness of the world in not attaining the Way lies in loving the high and loathing the low. Do they not know that the high places hold peril and the low places are safe, just as in digging a well: one does not dig toward the high, but the lower one goes, the more water there is. A person must do the same in his affairs — he must be down below, holding up the bottom and mending the leaks: what others do not want, you pick up; what others do not do, you do; what others detest, you do not mind. Like water seeking the low, one lifts up all things. Not seeking to be known by others, not relying on one's own strengths, not speaking of one's own merits — when the multitude submits to you, that is the Way.

In people's hearts there is always this preference for the high and the good. Do they not know that affairs are wholly ruined by the high and spoiled by the good? In the good and the high, where is the Way? People have not opened the right eye and have seen the Way amiss! What others do not do, you do; what others cast aside, you pick up — that is virtue, that is the Way. Like water seeking the low, lifting up all things, they will of themselves submit to you and of themselves obey you; this is called holding up the bottom. Alas, people all love to scramble upward and refuse to go down, so they are far from the Way!

To learn the Way, first learn to be low, and never cling to marks. I and Liu Zhenming first learned to beg for food — begging for three months, traveling two thousand li. A certain man followed Liu in learning the Way: when Liu lay down he lay down too, when Liu sat he sat too, never a step apart. Others said he would surely attain the Way. I said he would never attain it in this life! Because what he learned was a false outward form — it is too far from the Way!

The high are few and the low are many. If the Way you preach is high, how many lofty people are there? One must be able to be high and able to be low before one may be said to have the Way. If you cannot pierce through the high, you cannot succeed; if you cannot descend to the very bottom of the low, you cannot succeed.
In learning the Way I first learned to diminish and to be poor; others learned to be high and to lecture on scholarship, so they have not caught up with me.
Only contentment allows one to sink to the bottom; only contentment allows one to attain the Way. This is the essential secret of attaining the Way.
Loving the high is greed; fearing ruin is clinging; loving the good is karma; disliking what is not good is a lack of virtue; not fulfilling one's duty is losing the heavenly destiny.
This single word “good” has ruined all the heroes and the bold.

I often say that whether a person does affairs, studies, or learns the Way, he must first be sincere in intent — that is, single-minded, like the hungry seeking food and the thirsty thinking of drink: at every moment apply the mind, in every place devise the means, and only then can one succeed. In running the free schools for women, each time I suffered a blow I changed my method, and in the end I made clear the Way of women and pulled open the dark curtain that had covered womankind!

To awaken to the Way requires establishing a fixed resolve, and at every moment concentrating on awakening to a single Way; after a long time, the Way comes streaming in without end. Like a well-pump: the more you pump the more water flows, yet the pipe is very thin; the water is not inside the pipe but outside it — when the water in the pipe flows out, the water outside the pipe flows in to replenish it. The Way's coming without end is likewise.

My Way was not obtained all at once; it was gotten through investigating things little by little. When I did hired labor at my cousin Zhang's house, my cousin's son ordered me about at the work, and I investigated for a hundred days before I understood. Later I investigated matter by matter, and only then did I know that the source of the world is the maiden, the source of the world's order is the concubine, and the great mechanism of the world is money — without understanding these three matters, one cannot govern the world.

If a person wishes to understand the Way, he must first awaken to his own Way, then awaken to the Way of his family, then to the Way of all people, and only at the last examine the Way of all things. Where he does not know, he asks himself and answers himself, and in time he comes to understand — this is called questioning Heaven. While I was working as a hired laborer I asked myself: “Why do people work?” I answered myself: “To get through the days.” “Why get through the days?” “To keep people alive.” “Why keep people alive?” “To walk the Way.” When I thought it over carefully, I saw that the Way was not walked at all, and that everyone had taken up the wrong role! Only then did I investigate and bring forth the Way of the maiden, the Way of the old lady, and the Ways of father and son, husband and wife, and the rest — and this is what is called awakening to the Way.

The Way is the Way of Heaven; every person has it, and it has never been apart from anyone. Why then do people today not attain it? To give an example: a bean, once it has sprouted, must draw its sap upward, and only when the bean is fully formed does it count as done. A person too has a root; if he constantly reflects on his own root and seeks it in all sincerity for three months, he will attain it. This is what I attained when I sought the Way of working.

Whatever task a person does, whatever Way he walks, he can embrace heaven and earth and embrace all ages. Sadly, most people, once the thing is past, no longer know how to savor it. Whatever you have done, in your leisure you must ponder it; to ponder it until it is clear is called awakening, while to have done it and not know it is called delusion — and delusion is what a living being is. One who studies the Way must first examine what his body is doing, what his heart is holding, and what his nature is illuminating. When he has leisure, he should investigate whether what he did before was right or not, how he is acting now, and how he ought to act in the future. A person comprehends only as much as he can comprehend, and governs only as far as he can govern. In earlier days I did not understand, and so I grew angry and fell ill; only after I had pondered it clear did the illness pass.

Everything has its root, and the root of the Moral Society is man and woman. For the whole globe and all nations are made up of men and women; given men and women there are husbands and wives, and given husbands and wives there are the relations of father and son, elder and younger brother, friend and friend, ruler and minister. “The union of husband and wife is the beginning of human relations” — how true that saying is! If our Moral Society would rebuild society, it must first set to work on these two, man and woman, so that each may be established in his or her proper place and each stand on his or her own feet; then the five relations will of themselves be in order, the family will be regulated and the state well governed.

The Moral Society is empty; it must be filled with moral people, moral words, and moral deeds, and only then is it a true Moral Society. It is like a water vat: it must hold water to be a water vat, but if it holds sauce it becomes a sauce vat! So name and reality must match; this is of the greatest importance.
The members of the Moral Society, if they can expound morality and lead the customs of the age, are foremost in merit; if they cannot, they are the chief of sinners!

When the reforms of the late Qing failed, I knew that in time the scholars would all come under one house, and that in no more than fifty or sixty years it would turn into the new academic world. The scholars of the late Qing were all corrupt gentry, devoted to crooked ways, and so there arose a new academic world devoted to the overbearing. Now the overbearing has also gone out of fashion, and the compliant has come in its place; the Moral Society teaches only the compliant, and whatever comes is well. But if the Moral Society cannot take up the Way and expound it clearly, in the future it will still meet with calamity.

Morality and law are the two great functions of the state, yin and yang, and neither may be lacking. People today often say, “Morality makes up for what the law cannot reach.” They do not know that it is the law that makes up for what morality cannot reach; if morality is not made the master, then however strict the law, it will still fail.

The silkworm spins its cocoon not because it means to live inside it forever, but because it means to become a moth and fly out of it. A person's dealings should be the same. To found a society, open a school, run a business, or keep a household is not to grow old and die inside it — it is only to borrow it to accomplish my Way. People today take up one undertaking and treat it as the “retirement plot” for the second half of their lives; how foolish that is! When Zhang Yaxuan founded the Shuzhen Free Girls' School at Teng'aobao in Haicheng County, he ran it with great success, brought forth no small number of able people, and the school was no longer in difficulty. I urged him to leave and cut himself off from the school. The teachers, staff, and students all pleaded with him to stay, and he himself was unwilling to go. I said: “You are all too foolish! He is your leader; now that he has taught you to completion, if he does not go out and open the road, in the end you will all rot to death here!” I pressed him for more than twenty days, and only then did he leave Teng'aobao and go to the northern provinces to transform people; through this he came to understand the Way of the Four Great Realms (see Section 29, “The Four Great Realms”), and only then could the free girls' schools develop. Is this not a case in point?

However good the estate the ancestors built, it must still be ruined in the hands of their descendants. It is just like the religions founded by the teachers of old: however good they were, they too were ruined in the hands of their disciples, for none broke through the barrier of sons and younger brothers. Therefore I take no disciples and I am no master. My Way is the most equal of all: not being a master, I bear no blame; taking no disciples, I have no cares. How natural it is — and of course it is a dead end!

I have preached the Way to transform the world for forty years, and I know who believes and who does not. Some have believed for ten years, some for eight; those who do not believe I simply do not lead. When I lead people I lead them upward, whereas the ways of the world lead people downward — keeping an eye on them, managing them, and at the last resenting and hating them; outwardly it is watching over them, but in truth it is bullying them. I do not keep an eye even on my own wife and children; and though I do not watch over them for a time, I watch over them for all ages, for I can lead them into the heavenly halls and the Buddha land. Those who do not believe simply have shallow affinity — they must not be made into enemies. So in saving people one must also watch the heat of the fire.

After I attained the Way I passed it on to others; for if it were not passed on, I would bear the great guilt of the whole world. Though I have the Way, I do not sell the Way: I do not use the Way to support worldly living, nor use the Way to amass wealth. I am not afraid to beg for my food — I rely only on response. In earlier days the Moral Society had a membership fee; I opposed it, and it was abolished. At last year's conference they wanted to collect the fee again, and I said: “If you really do this, then this society will have no me in it.” Only then did they let the matter drop. In carrying out the Way we must not multiply branches and twigs, nor snatch people's wealth by clever tricks.

blocks.text: Section 28  Walking the Way and Doing Virtue

inline.s: The Way is walked and virtue is done; if you do not walk, there is no Way, and if you do not do, there is no virtue. Heaven names things according to heavenly principle; when a person acts according to his proper portion, he accords with the Way of Heaven, and what is done on the basis of the Way of Heaven is heavenly virtue, so that he can attain without thinking. People today know only how to seek wealth, not how to do virtue; that is to grasp the branch and let go the root — it is like a flower that blooms falsely, without having taken root: how could it bear fruit? Virtue is the root and wealth is the fruit. So if you wish to gain wealth, first do virtue; that virtue is the seed of the money tree. Hence it is said: “He who has great virtue will surely obtain his reward.”

There is no virtue gained by greed, no merit gained by contention, no blessing gained by stirring things up. To do a matter well and to help others accomplish their matters is merit, and one who has merit will surely hold authority. But if you boast of your own merit, contend for merit with others, or though your body does the work your heart is dissatisfied, that is called toiling without merit. To give money in charity or to urge others to goodness is both goodness; one who does good will surely be rich in the next life and enjoy great blessing — yet he is still within cause and effect. But if you can teach people to remove their habits, transform their inborn nature, and rid themselves of the afflictions of heart and nature, that is called saving the nature; saving the nature is a single rescue through all the ages, and that alone is virtue. Only when a person's nature is clear can he keep virtue.

For a clear-sighted person to hold up the foolish is called having virtue, and for the foolish to believe the clear-sighted is also having virtue. Heaven gave rise to the wise for the sake of the foolish. If the clear-sighted do not hold up the foolish, they defy the heavenly mandate; if the foolish do not believe the clear-sighted, they too defy the heavenly mandate. Though I have exhorted the world for many years, I still feel I have wronged everyone, because the people are not yet as clear-sighted as I am; if there were someone clearer than I, my heart would be at peace.

I often hear people say, “The great man can bend and stretch.” What does it mean to be able to bend and stretch? I hold that when you meet a foolish person, to be able to lower yourself beneath him and lift him up — only that counts as being able to bend; and when you meet a lofty person, to set your aspiration above his and not be overawed by him — only that is called being able to stretch.
