To establish many works and form many human ties is outer merit, and only with outer merit is there inner fruit. To fulfill the human relations and carry out public good are both outer merit. It is like a plant: putting down roots, growing a trunk, putting out branches and leaves, and blossoming are all outer merit, and only when the outer merit is complete can it bear inner fruit. If a person has no outer merit, he cannot accomplish inner fruit. Take two men preaching the Way: the one who does not put it into practice may speak with a shower of heavenly flowers, and no one will pay attention — he may even be slandered; while the one who puts it into practice, whatever he says, others believe, and even if it is a common saying, his hearers feel there is a Way in it. Is this not clear proof that only with outer merit is there inner fruit?
As many people as admire you, so great is your virtue; as many people as believe and submit to you, so great is your merit.

The people of the world all fear deep water and scorching fire, and fear to die in them. Do they not know that the lover of fame dies by fame and the lover of profit dies by profit, and that they stand in deep water and scorching fire every day without even knowing it? In my preaching of the Way, not wanting fame is to “enter fire without being burned,” and not wanting money is to “enter water without drowning.”

Morality has flowed on without cease from ancient times to the present, yet it has gone lower and lower, until it has sunk beneath the water! What is the water? It is the money that people love; for the sake of money they destroy their conscience and lose the Way as well! The reason I could become a good man, and the reason everyone admires me, is simply that I have broken off all dealings with money.

The person who studies the Way but does not go and learn from the Buddha, and instead first goes to repair temples, has let the Buddha send him far away! The student who only reads and does not put it into practice has let the books send him far away! The student of morality who only talks of the Way and does not walk it has let the Way send him far away! When I learn of one person of old, I learn that one person of old; when I learn of one person of today, I learn that one person of today; when I learn one word, I put that one word into practice. Only that is “the unity of knowledge and action.”
To deceive others is sin, to burden others is guilt, to help others is merit, and to bring others to completion is virtue. Ask yourself often: what sort of person am I?

I often say, “Overturn the world and create the Great Unity.” Everyone laughs at me and says I am talking big. In truth this saying is not big at all; it is only because they do not know how the overturning is to be done that they call it big talk. “Great matters must be handled in a small way, and small matters in a great way” is also something I often say. Overturning the world is indeed a great matter, but it must be begun from a small place. How small? As small as a mote of dust. And what is that small? It is a person's thought. If you can overturn a person's thought, turning the selfish into the public and the crooked into the upright, is the world not overturned?

I often say, “Great matters must be handled in a small way, and small matters in a great way.” To bring peace to the world is a great matter, yet it must be begun from the state, from the state to the family, from the family to the person, from the person to the heart, from the heart to the intent, and from the intent to extending knowledge and investigating things — is this not shrinking it down to the very smallest? I am a farmer, exceedingly foolish and dull, who never spent a single day in school, and when I say I would overturn the world and create the Great Unity, everyone laughs at me for talking big. In truth it is they who have not understood the meaning of the Great Learning. If one can shrink it down to the intent and begin from making the intent sincere, what difficulty is there in bringing peace to the world? Ordinary people also think that bringing peace to the world is the business of princes and lords; but I hold that one must begin at the root, from little children, instilling the spirit of morality from childhood and spreading it through the world — can the world then fail to be at peace?

Will, intent, heart, and body are the Four Great Realms. Superstitious people say that on the Bridge of Helplessness there are three roads: one of gold, one of silver, and one the road to the Yellow Springs. I say that to be a person by the will is “gold,” to be a person by the intent is “silver,” and to act by heart and body is to have set foot on the “road to the Yellow Springs.”

The person of the realm of will does not speak (he has no complaint, and however things are, all is well); the person of the realm of intent is content; the person of the realm of heart is greedy; the person of the realm of body loves to fight. The one who does not speak is called the person without heart; the contented one is called the person of pure heart; the greedy one is called the person of worried heart; and the one who loves to fight is called the person of spoiled heart. The spoiled heart is a ghost, the worried heart is a human being, the pure heart is a spirit, and the heartless is a Buddha.

The person of the realm of body thinks only of making plans for his body; he has himself and no one else, is overbearing and unreasonable, and whatever he sees he wants to make his own; when he cannot get the advantage he grows angry and comes to blows, and he is forever fretting — therefore he is a “ghost.” The person of the realm of heart is greedy beyond repletion and never content, his whole mind full of delusive thoughts, fond of scheming and clever calculation — therefore he is a petty man. The person of the realm of intent is content and always joyous, and joy is “spirit.” The person of the realm of will has no complaint about anything and sees through cause and effect, seeking no further round of rebirth — so the one without complaint counts as a “Buddha.” If a person would transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, he must know how to shift his realm.

I often say that a person must distinguish the Four Great Realms clearly. Just how is one to distinguish them clearly? If one can keep one's true nature thus-immovable, and hold up the foolish of the world so that they become people of great wisdom, that is the realm of will, the realm of the Buddha land. If one can keep the heart free of a single thing and be always joyous and free of care, that is the realm of intent, the realm of the heavenly halls. If one is greedy beyond repletion, full of cares and anxieties, that is the realm of heart, the realm of the sea of suffering. If one contends and grasps, stirs and disturbs for the sake of fame and profit, indulges in wine and women, lingers and forgets to return, and loves bravery and fighting, that is the realm of body, the realm of hell. Therefore I say: the realm of will is the Buddha land, the realm of intent is the heavenly halls, the realm of heart is the sea of suffering, and the realm of body is hell.

To be settled in the realm of will is the Buddha land: however the circumstances may be, good or bad, poor or rich, gaining or losing, honored or disgraced, living or dying, one can remain thus-immovable and think only of benefiting others and bringing others to completion, being a person by the will. To be settled in the realm of intent is the heavenly halls: to be content and always joyous is to be a living immortal. The heart is the human realm: much thinking and much worrying, anxious over gain and loss — that is the boundless sea of suffering. People today make the heart their master; how then can they become Buddhas? The body is a thing born of the womb and will perish in the end, so it must be seen as false. A person must establish merit and establish virtue; if he does not know to begin from merit and virtue, how can he accomplish the Way?

The person of the realm of will is like spring, devoted to giving life. The ancients said, “To have cause for anger yet not grow angry dissolves the demons; to have a grievance yet not requite it is practice.” That is precisely the mark of the person of the realm of will. The person of the realm of intent is like summer, devoted to containing and nurturing, so that all things grow and flourish; “the noble man completes the good of others” — that is precisely the conduct of the person of the realm of intent. The person of the realm of heart is like autumn, devoted to selfishness: just as at the autumn harvest all things bear their own fruit without regard for others, so everything is left scattered and broken. The person of the realm of body is like winter, devoted to destruction: he knows only to seize by force and snatch by robbery, and everyone fears him and dares not touch him, for at the slightest contact one suffers no small harm. Therefore I often say that the realms of will and intent build the world, while the realms of heart and body destroy it.

The will has the nature of will: it does nothing and yet leaves nothing undone. The intent has the nature of intent: it trusts people, and when good things come it is willing to yield them to others. The heart has the nature of heart: it is greedy without repletion, single-mindedly for itself, always wanting to take advantage of others. The body has the nature of body: it is destructive by habit, and though both itself and others are harmed, it does not know remorse. Therefore the realms of heart and body must never be allowed to be master; they may only be made to obey.

When the matter is spoiled but the person is not, that is a person of the realm of will, who reckons nothing against anyone. The person of the realm of intent contains all with great righteousness. The person of the realm of heart is always scheming how to take advantage. The person of the realm of body grows red-eyed at the sight of things, and when he cannot get them in hand he grows angry.

The Buddha spoke of three thousand great thousand worlds; I say there are four great worlds, and one who has attained the Way sees at a glance to which realm a person belongs. Whoever makes the body his person, no matter how far he rises, is a shatterer of the family fortune; whoever makes the heart his person, no matter how capable, is a person of worried heart; whoever makes the intent his person, no matter how many his affairs, does not weary his heart, and is a living immortal; whoever makes the will his person, no matter how adverse the circumstances he meets, does not stir his nature, and is a Buddha. (Seen from the Buddha Dharma, the fruit of unmoved karma is recompense in the heavens of the form and formless realms, and has not yet transcended the round of rebirth. If one can dedicate this merit to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one will surely be reborn in the Western Pure Land and become a Buddha beyond doubt.)

When the person of the realm of body speaks, the words are done as soon as they are out, and he does not keep them at all — they are empty. When the person of the realm of heart speaks, he loves to talk of empty principle, and having spoken he does not act — it is false. When the person of the realm of intent speaks, once spoken he does not forget and will surely carry it out — it is good. When the person of the realm of will speaks, it is like a nail driven into a board, which cannot be pulled out even by force — it is true.

The body is bad, the heart is false, the intent is good, and the will is true. If a person becomes true, then Buddhas, spirits, human beings, and ghosts can all be moved — this is called “one truth, all truth.” If you are not true, then all is false, and even a good thing will turn false. Therefore the noble man seeks it in himself and does not resent others. That others are not true is because I am not true; that others are not good is because I am not good; that the world is not good is also because I am not good. The Great Learning says, “When one family is humane, one state grows humane.” That is why I acknowledge the faults of the whole world as my own.

People push all their faults outward and do not know to examine themselves; hence disputes arise. The person of the realm of body does not know he has faults, and when he hears of a fault he grows angry, and to the end of his life does not change. The person of the realm of heart loves face, and when he hears of a fault he glosses it over: this is to conceal the fault, knowing it but not correcting it. The person of the realm of intent is humble, and when he hears of a fault he is glad, and having a fault he can correct it. The person of the realm of will bows when he hears of a fault and is grateful in his heart; he acknowledges the fault from the heart, not with the lips — he truly acknowledges it, and repents within.

The will is like the root of a tree, the intent like the trunk, the heart like the branching boughs, and the body like the leaves and twigs. The leaves and twigs and the branching boughs must be pruned, and therefore it is said, “rectify the heart and cultivate the person.”

Between the Four Great Realms of will, intent, heart, and body lie a hundred and eight thousand li. The person of the realm of body will stop at nothing, and he has a pack of bad friends for eating, drinking, and pleasure; even if he wants to learn to be good, that pack of bad friends will pester him so that he cannot advance — so shifting realms is very hard. When the realm of heart would climb to the realm of intent, the relatives and friends of the realm of heart pull it back; when the realm of intent would climb to the realm of will, the relatives and friends of the realm of intent pull it back. Therefore one must distinguish the Four Great Realms clearly before one can accomplish the Way. Since I took up the Shande Dang, I have climbed several steps in a row. Sun Wukong can cover a hundred and eight thousand li in one somersault of his cloud — I have that same skill. When the Shande Dang I ran failed, the matter was spoiled but the person was not: that was one somersault of a hundred and eight thousand li. After the Anda conference, when Gao Zhengwu and Du Shaopeng wanted to repay me the Shande Dang debts, I would not accept: that was another somersault of a hundred and eight thousand li.

The Four Great Realms are given to place people. If you understand the Four Great Realms, you understand every person: you know from which realm he came and in which realm he now rests. Whoever belongs to a realm does the work of that realm. Whether he has a root from former lives, whether he has cause and effect, whether his nature is good or evil, is all carried in his nature; “sincere within, it takes form without,” and a person of clear nature can see it at a glance. Not only can one know his present, but one can know his former life as well, and what he will be reborn as in the life to come.

I say the six paths of rebirth are all here in our own bodies! Why seek them outside? In the way a person holds himself and acts: to use the will is the Buddha path, to use the intent is the spirit path, to use the heart is the human path, to grasp at outer things without regard for feeling or principle is the path of things, to be devoted to flaring up in anger is the path of demons, and to be devoted to resentment is the path of ghosts. These six paths turn in rebirth within our bodies every day; why wait until after death to know them?

A person must comprehend the Four Great Realms of will, intent, heart, and body before he can save all living beings. If he knows only how spirits are made and how human beings are born, but does not know how animals come to be, he cannot save the animals. The nature of the ox has a foolish fire within it; the nature of the dog has yin wood within it; the nature of the chicken has yin metal and lacks earth, having lacked honest faith in a former life — and so it appears in that kind of body and suffers that kind of hardship. If we do not know its origin, how can we save it from suffering?

The will is the Buddha path, the intent is the spirit path, the heart is the human path, and to lose one's temper is the ghost path. Lose your temper and the spirit scatters; set up the will and the Buddha comes. But the ghost path, being unclear, does not recognize people; the human path, being unmastered, does not recognize spirits; and the spirit path, being unclear, does not recognize the Buddha. If a person can restore his heavenly nature, he knows all things and every calamity dissolves. If he settles the intent in sincerity, all things become spiritual and every affliction ceases; if he settles the heart, all things are penetrated and every difficulty ceases; if he trains the body well, he can do every kind of work and find affinity everywhere — and the Buddha land appears before him.

One who knows how to use the will is the more joyous the more he meets adversity; one who knows how to use the intent, however great his intent, has a righteousness to match it; one who knows how to use the heart has a heart of a thousand transformations and inexhaustible subtle uses; one who knows how to use the body, however he labors, never injures himself with the labor.

When I was keeping vigil at the grave, I kept it to a hundred days, and kept vigil over the Three Realms, and all the Buddhas and all the patriarchs came to join in and match their names. Only with a sincere will can one gather the Buddhas; only with a sincere intent can one gather the spirits; only with a sincere heart can one gather people; only with a perfected body can one gather things. Whichever realm is sincere, that realm is spiritual. I pondered upward to the Buddha land and downward to hell, and I do not know how many times a day I pondered.

When my son asked me for money, I said, “Very well!” I neither grew angry nor rejoiced, because I was settled in the realm of will and had no complaint about anything. When Xu Ruilin's son asked him for money, he smiled and said, “If I had money, on whom would I spend it but you? It is a pity I have none.” He was a man of the realm of intent. When Wang Guohua's son wrote asking for money, he flew into a great rage and tore the letter to pieces; he was a man of the realm of heart. When Tu Yongnian's son asked him for money, not only did he not give it, he worked himself into a fury and died of it; he was a man of the realm of body.

The body is a thing that suffers, yet people set great store by it, making plans for it at every turn, cherishing and protecting it in life, and after death wanting a golden burial and a jade burial; and it is to preserve the physical body that graves are dug and tombs are robbed. How foolish the people of the world are! Of things that have form, which can escape decay? The body is a thing that undergoes calamity; when it is spoiled, that is the end of it, and it cannot be counted on. Only by making it work can its sins be ended; if you make it enjoy blessings, how can its sins be ended? If they are not ended in this life, there will be another round of rebirth.

The heart is a demon, appearing everywhere. A thousand thoughts and ten thousand calculations, wild and delusive imaginings — that is the demon troubling the heart. Care and worry, anger and flaring up — that is the demon troubling the nature. Idling about with a body full of cravings — that is the demon troubling the body. The harm the demon does makes the heart grow cold. I was fortunate enough to awaken quickly and pinched the heart to death, making the will my master; only so did I leave suffering and attain joy!

In spring look at the seed, in summer look at the sprout. A seed that is six-tenths good, planted in the ground, will still come up and grow vigorously; but when autumn comes it turns into a wild grass seed, and when the harvest time comes the wild seed falls to the ground first, and the next year the field will surely be waste. The people of the world who use the heart are seeds that will not make the grade. People today have all become “wild grass seed” — how can the world fail to be in disorder?

The person who uses the heart is like one baking a pancake in a pan: a little too much fire and it is scorched. The person who uses the intent is like one steaming a cake in a bamboo steamer: however great the steam, it is not spoiled.
When there is weariness in the heart, there is weariness in the destiny, and in fact there will surely be wearying affairs.

To be displeased is to have grown a little eye! The intent is like a rubber ball: let it have a hole the size of a needle's eye, and the air leaks out. The nature is the root and the will is the base, the root of all things and all affairs. The root is like rain: the rain of heaven has no intention of its own, yet the sour pear that receives it must turn sour, and the licorice that receives it must turn sweet. The will, between heaven and earth, is like that rain as well.

When we observe the deeds of the ancients, we must ask by which of the four — will, intent, heart, or body — they accomplished the Way. Mencius's mother, in teaching her son, accomplished it by the word “will”; the Third Lady, in teaching her son, accomplished it by the word “intent.” In observing people of today it is the same.
Good, good: finish one and good one, good one and open one. With the body, the heart cannot be let go; with the heart, the intent cannot be let go; with the intent, the will cannot be let go.

To draw near to those near you is the heart; to draw near to those far from you is the intent. The spirit draws near to those far off and keeps far from those near. The Buddha keeps far from all, and being far, is not far. Take how the people of the world treat me: are they not all near ones to me now?

The intent is the spirit. Settle the intent in sincerity and do not let it scatter outward; nourish it long, and it will of itself be like a spirit. The spirit is as great as heaven and earth: wherever a thought arises, there it is; whoever thinks of it, to him it is spiritual. The intent is sunlight: it can pierce the darkness, and when private desires are wholly cleansed, heavenly principle flows of itself.

When the inborn nature is transformed, that is the intent. In transforming the world we use the intent for lighter cases and the will for heavier ones. One who can use the will has the sins of ten thousand ages wiped out with a single stroke. But when the demon comes you must be able to hold firm; stir ever so slightly, and that is a seed.

People must be cautious in holding themselves and walking the Way: once a person of the realm of will lets his will topple, he falls to the realm of body; and once a person of the realm of intent makes a false step, he falls to the realm of heart.

If you would settle the will firmly, you must nourish the body with the Three Realms. First you must establish the root. A teacher, for instance, should constantly study the Way of teaching, drilling through the principles of the books, and the root will of itself be established.

If a person is settled in the realm of will, thus-immovable, you need not go seeking the Buddha — the Buddha will come seeking you. If you cannot settle the will, then though you pray to the Buddha every day, the Buddha will pay you no heed. For when you see a good thing and your heart rejoices, you have been toppled by the demon of good; and when you see a bad thing and your heart frets, you have been toppled by the demon of evil! But if you reach the realm of will, and good and bad alike do not stir your heart, and right and wrong alike do not stir your nature, then the demon will help you become a Buddha!

People who practice fear the dust of the world, and so some leave the dust and some avoid it. Do they not know that the dust is in the heart and not outside the body, and must be settled from within the heart? The heart must have no dust, but outside the body there cannot but be dust. To be neither deluded nor defiled, to meet the demon without regret, to suffer wrong without resenting anyone, and to let gain and loss, suffering and joy alike leave the heart unmoved — only that is to be a person of the realm of will.

Only when the heart is dead can the nature be transformed; when the inborn nature is transformed, then the intent is sincere; when the intent is sincere, then the will is sincere — this is a fixed principle.

At first I settled in the realm of intent, and truly it was spiritual! But I thought it too small, and settled in the will instead: no complaint about anything, earning no money and spending none, devoted wholly to preaching the Way, seeking everything within the Way — living, I live in the Way; dying, I die in the Way.

In using the will one must begin from what is close at hand: whoever I am near, I first awaken to his Way and first understand his nature, and I lift him up until he is won over. First make one or two people won over, then make a thousand or a hundred won over — only that is truly using the will.

To be a person by the will is to have no complaint and no change: you may bully me and scold me, and it still completes me; you may be false and you may cheat, and it still completes me; even if you kill me, it still completes me. Yue Fei, for instance, was brought to completion by Qin Hui.
The spirit helps people, the ghost stirs people up. If one can settle the will firmly, not only can the spirit help, the ghost can help too — and help from the opposite side has greater power.
The will must be high, the intent great, the heart level, and the body low.

Among the sages of every religion, there is not one who did not make the will his master. I have heard that Confucius, when the grain ran out in Chen, remained calm and at ease, singing and playing his lute without cease; and I have heard that Jesus, nailed to the cross, rose again on the third day and still saved the people of the world; and that Śākyamuni Buddha, when he was the Ascetic of Patience, had his limbs cut off by King Kali, and still said: “When I become a Buddha, I will save you first!” Is this spirit of theirs one and the same? Therefore I say that though the forms of the religions differ, this spirit is the same; to divide them into separate schools and categories is quite wrong!
When one truly reaches the realm of will, there is not a spark of temper left — only true joy remains!

When I was young, I often heard relatives and friends say that both my father and my grandfather were scholars, and that my great-grandfather had the fine name of a man of “books of virtue” — and yet I had never spent a day in school, and might be called wholly illiterate! With what face would I meet my ancestors underground? Thinking of this, I felt deeply ashamed! So I set up my will: however poor I might be, I must put my son through school! Afterwards my son studied from the age of eight, was very clever, and was greatly praised by his teacher. When I saw that both my forebears and my descendants could study, what was I to do? So I vowed to myself that I too must study, without fail! From the age of thirty-eight I learned to preach the books of virtue, and afterward I too could recognize a few characters and could preach the books of virtue; and now I can study morality together with everyone — thinking back on it, what joy! All of this came from setting up the will.

People often say a person must have a great root and a great vessel. What is the “great root”? When I was young and working as a hired laborer, I heard someone tell the Romance of the Three Kingdoms and say, “Lord Guan will not leave Cao's camp until he has won an inch of merit.” So I set up a will — no matter for whom I hired out, I too would not leave Cao's camp until I had won an inch of merit. Setting up the will is the “great root.” What is the “great vessel”? Before doing a thing, you must think: can this be put into practice throughout the world, and if everyone in the world did it, would it be good? If it would be good, it will certainly work — that is the “great vessel.” People today look only to power and influence, which is a great mistake.

When I was thirty-five, I already knew that the post-heavenly world had reached its final decline, and that in time it would become the pre-heavenly world! How then do the pre-heavenly and the post-heavenly differ? Everyone who cares only for his wife and children belongs to the post-heavenly; whoever disregards home and family and seeks only the common good belongs to the pre-heavenly. When I was twenty-one and working as a hired laborer, I saw some brothers dividing up the family estate, taking up knives and guns over the inheritance, and there were even cases that ended in loss of life. I wondered to myself, for whom were they contending? I thought about it for a whole day, and then suddenly I understood: they were contending for their wives and sons! At that moment I was carrying dung, and I threw the dung basket onto the pile and said loudly, 'I must become an extraordinary person!' My companions stared at me, not knowing what I meant. When I reached thirty-eight and was keeping vigil at the grave, I said to the women of the family, 'From now on I can no longer run the household for you.' When the period of grave-keeping came to an end, I took exhorting people to goodness and establishing learning as my life's calling, and I have done so up to the present day.

When the Meng family of Mengjiatun in Jinxi County rebuilt the Temple of Mother Meng, the undertaking was enormous. Upon its completion I went to visit and met Meng Laofeng, the temple's manager. I made him a deep bow, but he paid me no attention; I spoke to him, but he gave no answer. As I walked out of the temple I made a vow: 'So the Meng family produced a sage, and you are so arrogant! May the Wang family not also produce a sage? I must resolve to learn to become a sage!' A bystander jeered at me, saying, 'Can you ever catch up to her?' I replied, 'Even if I cannot catch up, I will walk a few steps after her!'

I heard someone explain that the Doctrine of the Mean says, 'Filial piety consists in well carrying on the aims of one's fathers and well setting forth their deeds.' That is spoken of one's own forebears, but I think it can be extended further. I heard the story of 'Yang Jiao'ai giving up his life to fully preserve friendship,' and so I carried on Yang Jiao'ai's aim and went to rescue the good person Yang Bai, thereby also setting forth Yang Jiao'ai's deed. In doing this I turned from ignorance to clarity. Whose aim among the sages and worthies may one not carry on? Whoever carries on the aim of a sage or worthy — is he not a 'filial son'?

In the world today, all the gods and spirits are present among human beings, yet they have not been born again and descended into the world. Whose aim you seize, that one's spiritual radiance comes to you; whichever deity you emulate, that deity's spirit arrives; whichever sage or worthy you emulate, that sage or worthy's spirit arrives. Whatever matter you meet, learn from the one who embodies it — like picking flowers: pluck one, do one. Mencius said, 'Every person can become Yao or Shun'; this is precisely to bid people seize an aim. If an ordinary person never seizes the aim of the ancients, he remains an ordinary person to the end.
